# How to use this guide

The subject has 13 units that follow the 13 chapters of the ER-2020 syllabus. Units 1–3 are analytical and inorganic chemistry; Unit 4 is naming of compounds; Units 5–13 are drug monographs (class, chemical name, structure of starred drugs, uses, stability, storage, dosage forms and brands).

Study plan: one unit a day. Read the notes, write each starred structure once from memory, then answer the question bank without looking. Finish with the MCQs of that unit.

**Typical ER-2020 D.Pharm theory paper (80 marks, 3 hours) + 20 marks sessional.** Boards and universities following the PCI Education Regulations 2020 commonly use the pattern below. Confirm the exact pattern with your college, because a board may change the number of questions.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective questions (MCQs / fill in the blanks / one word) – all compulsory | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Short answers – attempt 10 of 11 | 10 × 3 = 30 |
| C | Long answers – attempt 6 of 7 | 6 × 5 = 30 |

In this app, **long** questions carry 5 marks and **short** questions 3 marks to match this pattern. **Very-short** (2-mark) questions are for quick revision and viva.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** – asked in most years or carries large syllabus weight (limit tests, titration types, antacids, starred CNS/ANS drugs, anti-TB, antimalarials, penicillins).
- **Medium** – asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** – rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates based on syllabus hours and common question patterns. They are not a promise.

**Where the marks are (syllabus hours out of 75)**

| Units | Hours | Share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Errors and limit tests, 2 Volumetric analysis | 8 + 8 | ~21% |
| 3 Inorganic pharmaceuticals | 7 | ~9% |
| 5 CNS, 6 ANS | 9 + 9 | ~24% |
| 11 Anti-infectives, 12 Antibiotics | 8 + 8 | ~21% |
| 7 CVS, 8 Diuretics, 9 Hypoglycaemics, 10 Analgesics, 13 Anticancer, 4 Nomenclature | 5 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 2 | ~25% |

**Scoring tips for Pharmaceutical Chemistry**

1. **For a drug monograph answer use the same order every time:** class → chemical name → structure (if starred) → mechanism (one line) → uses → adverse effects → stability and storage → dosage forms/brands. Examiners give a mark for each heading.
2. **Draw structures neatly** with the key group labelled (e.g. "Cl at C-2" for chlorpromazine, "5,5-diphenyl" for phenytoin). If unsure of a full structure, draw the nucleus and label the substituents in words; that still earns part marks.
3. **For limit tests** always write: principle with equation → reagents and their role → procedure in a two-column table (test vs standard) → observation → result ("passes if…").
4. **For titrations** write the principle, the equation, the indicator with its colour change, and one pharmaceutical example.
5. **Storage is a favourite exam point**: light-sensitive (adrenaline, chlorpromazine, frusemide, nifedipine, silver nitrate), moisture-sensitive (aspirin, ferrous sulphate, carbamazepine), refrigerated (insulin, amphotericin B, reconstituted amoxicillin syrup, vinblastine), not refrigerated (5-FU, cisplatin solution).
6. **Learn one brand name per drug** – the syllabus asks for "popular brand names".
7. In MCQs, watch for pairs that are easily confused: iodimetry vs iodometry, Mohr vs Volhard, chlorpromazine (phenothiazine) vs haloperidol (butyrophenone), imipramine (N in ring) vs amitriptyline (C= in ring), primaquine (8-amino) vs chloroquine (4-amino).

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only one hour, learn these with full answers: **limit test for iron and arsenic**, **types of titration (non-aqueous, complexometric, precipitation, redox)**, **antacids**, **chlorpromazine, phenytoin, diazepam**, **propranolol and atropine**, **INH and chloroquine**, **penicillin nucleus and amoxicillin**, **aspirin and paracetamol**, **cyclophosphamide and cisplatin**.

## Analysis (Units 1–2)

| Test / titration | Key reagent | Indicator / effect | Key point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Limit test chloride | AgNO3 + dilute HNO3 | Opalescence | Away from light |
| Limit test sulphate | BaCl2 reagent + dilute HCl | Turbidity | Alcohol + K2SO4 seeding |
| Limit test iron | Thioglycollic acid + citric acid + NH3 | Purple | Reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ |
| Limit test heavy metals | H2S / sulphide, pH 3–4 | Brown | ppm of lead |
| Limit test arsenic | Zn + HCl, KI, SnCl2 | Stain on HgCl2 paper | Lead acetate cotton traps H2S |
| Acid–base | NaOH / HCl | Phenolphthalein, methyl orange | Weak acid → phenolphthalein |
| Non-aqueous (bases) | HClO4 in glacial acetic acid | Crystal violet | Mercuric acetate for halides |
| Non-aqueous (acids) | Sodium methoxide | Thymol blue | DMF solvent |
| Mohr | AgNO3, neutral | K2CrO4 → red-brown | Direct |
| Volhard | Excess AgNO3, back with NH4SCN | Ferric alum → red | Acid; nitrobenzene in modified |
| Fajans | AgNO3 | Fluorescein, eosin | Adsorption |
| Complexometric | EDTA (1 : 1) | Eriochrome black T wine red → blue | pH 10 buffer |
| Permanganometry | KMnO4 + H2SO4 | Self indicator | Not HCl |
| Iodimetry / iodometry | I2 / thiosulphate | Starch | Direct / indirect |

- **Accuracy** = near true value (systematic errors). **Precision** = repeats agree (random errors).
- **Primary standards:** KHP, Na2CO3, oxalic acid, K2Cr2O7, NaCl.
- **Gravimetry:** precipitate → digest → filter → wash → ignite → weigh; gravimetric factor.

## Inorganic (Unit 3)

| Compound | One-line fact |
| --- | --- |
| Ferrous sulphate | FeSO4·7H2O; oxidises in moist air – airtight |
| Ferrous fumarate | ~33% iron, stable |
| Ferric ammonium citrate | Deliquescent, light sensitive; syrups |
| Ferrous ascorbate | Better absorbed; Orofer XT |
| Carbonyl iron | Elemental Fe, slow release, safer in overdose |
| Al(OH)3 / Mg(OH)2 | Constipation / diarrhoea → combined; magaldrate = both in one |
| NaHCO3 | Systemic antacid, alkalosis, CO2 |
| CaCO3 | Acid rebound, milk-alkali syndrome |
| Dilute HCl | Achlorhydria, through a straw |
| MgSO4 | Saline purgative; eclampsia |
| H2O2 | 6% = 20 volume; cool, dark, vented cap |
| Bleaching powder | ≥30% available chlorine; airtight |
| KMnO4 | 1 : 1,000–1 : 10,000 oxidising antiseptic |
| Chlorhexidine | Bisbiguanide; inactivated by soap |
| NaF | Fluorapatite – anticaries; fluorosis |
| O2 / N2O / CO2 | Black-white shoulder / blue / grey; no oil on O2 |

## Nomenclature (Unit 4)

Hantzsch–Widman: oxa > thia > aza; stems -irine (3), -ete (4), -ole (5), -ine (6), -epine (7); saturated N rings -iridine, -etidine, -olidine, -inane.

## Classic adverse effects (one word each)

Phenytoin – gum hypertrophy · Valproate – liver, neural tube defects · Chlorpromazine – photosensitivity · Haloperidol – EPS · Captopril – dry cough · Amiodarone – thyroid/lung · Frusemide – hypokalaemia, ototoxicity · Spironolactone – gynaecomastia · Metformin – lactic acidosis, B12 · Glibenclamide – hypoglycaemia · Aspirin – Reye's syndrome · Paracetamol – liver (NAPQI) · INH – neuropathy (B6) · Ethambutol – optic neuritis · Rifampicin – orange urine · Primaquine/dapsone – G6PD haemolysis · Chloroquine – retinopathy · Tetracycline – teeth staining · Chloramphenicol – grey baby, aplastic anaemia · Clindamycin – pseudomembranous colitis · Cyclophosphamide – haemorrhagic cystitis · Cisplatin – nephrotoxicity · Doxorubicin – cardiotoxicity · Vinblastine – fatal intrathecal.

## Storage hot-list

- **Protect from light:** catecholamines, chlorpromazine, frusemide, nifedipine, silver nitrate, sulphacetamide drops, cisplatin, amphotericin B.
- **Keep dry / airtight:** aspirin, ferrous sulphate, ferric ammonium citrate, sodium valproate, carbamazepine, bleaching powder.
- **Refrigerate (2–8 °C):** insulin (never freeze), amphotericin B, reconstituted amoxicillin syrup, chloramphenicol eye drops (before opening), vinblastine.
- **Do not refrigerate:** fluorouracil, cisplatin solution, mannitol 20%.

practicals.markdown:
# Limit test for chlorides

**Aim:** To perform the limit test for chlorides on the given sample (for example sodium bicarbonate, potassium chloride-free salts or any IP substance) as per the Indian Pharmacopoeia.

> Quantities of sample and standard are given in each IP monograph. Follow your lab manual and teacher where they differ. Wear a lab coat and goggles.

## Principle

Chloride ions react with silver nitrate in the presence of dilute nitric acid to give silver chloride. In the small amounts allowed, AgCl appears as a faint **opalescence**, not a precipitate. The opalescence of the sample is compared with that produced by a known amount of chloride (standard) under identical conditions.

Cl⁻ + AgNO3 → AgCl (white opalescence) + NO3⁻

Dilute nitric acid keeps the medium acidic so that carbonate, phosphate or hydroxide do not precipitate with silver, and it gives a uniform opalescence.

## Requirements

Two matched Nessler cylinders (50 ml), dilute nitric acid, 0.1 M silver nitrate, standard chloride solution (dilute NaCl, e.g. 0.05845% w/v), chloride-free distilled water, glass rods, black tile or paper.

## Procedure

| Step | Test cylinder | Standard cylinder |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Dissolve the specified weight of sample in water | Take the specified volume of standard NaCl solution |
| 2 | Add 10 ml dilute nitric acid | Add 10 ml dilute nitric acid |
| 3 | Dilute to 50 ml with water | Dilute to 50 ml with water |
| 4 | Add 1 ml 0.1 M silver nitrate, stir with a glass rod | Same |
| 5 | Keep 5 minutes protected from direct sunlight | Same |

6. View both cylinders from above (down the length) against a black background and compare the opalescence.

## Observation

| Cylinder | Opalescence |
| --- | --- |
| Test | Less / more than standard |
| Standard | Reference |

## Result

The given sample **passes / fails** the limit test for chlorides (passes if its opalescence is not more than the standard).

## Precautions

1. Use chloride-free water and clean cylinders rinsed with distilled water.
2. Add reagents to both cylinders in the same order and at the same time.
3. Protect from direct light (silver chloride darkens).
4. Stir both cylinders equally; compare against a black background.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is nitric acid added?** To prevent precipitation of other silver salts and give uniform opalescence.
2. **Why not hydrochloric acid?** It contains chloride and would give a false positive.
3. **Why compare against a black background?** White opalescence is seen best on black.
4. **What is a Nessler cylinder?** A flat-bottomed glass cylinder marked at 50 ml, used for comparing colour or turbidity.
5. **Is a limit test quantitative?** It is semi-quantitative: it only shows whether the impurity is below the permitted limit.
practicals.title: Limit test for chlorides

practicals.markdown:
# Limit test for sulphates

**Aim:** To perform the limit test for sulphates on the given sample as per the Indian Pharmacopoeia.

> Use the sample weight and standard volume given in the monograph. Follow your lab manual and teacher where they differ.

## Principle

Sulphate ions react with barium chloride in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid to give a **turbidity of barium sulphate**. The turbidity of the sample is compared with that of a standard containing a known amount of sulphate.

SO4²⁻ + BaCl2 → BaSO4 (white turbidity) + 2Cl⁻

- **Dilute HCl** prevents precipitation of barium carbonate, phosphate or oxalate.
- **Barium sulphate reagent** contains barium chloride, sulphate-free alcohol and a small amount of potassium sulphate. Alcohol prevents supersaturation; potassium sulphate provides seed crystals so turbidity forms quickly and evenly.

## Requirements

Nessler cylinders, dilute hydrochloric acid, barium sulphate reagent, standard sulphate solution (potassium sulphate, e.g. 0.1089% w/v), distilled water, glass rods.

## Procedure

| Step | Test | Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Dissolve specified quantity of sample in water in a Nessler cylinder | Specified volume of standard potassium sulphate solution |
| 2 | Add 2 ml dilute HCl | Add 2 ml dilute HCl |
| 3 | Dilute to 45 ml with water | Dilute to 45 ml with water |
| 4 | Add 5 ml barium sulphate reagent, stir | Same |
| 5 | Keep for 5 minutes | Same |

6. Compare the turbidity by viewing down the cylinders against a black background.

## Observation

Turbidity in test cylinder is less / more than the standard.

## Result

The given sample **passes / fails** the limit test for sulphates.

## Precautions

1. Use sulphate-free water and clean apparatus.
2. Use freshly prepared barium sulphate reagent.
3. Treat test and standard identically and simultaneously.
4. Stir both equally; compare after the same time.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is alcohol present in barium sulphate reagent?** To prevent supersaturation and give uniform turbidity.
2. **Role of potassium sulphate in the reagent?** Seeding for rapid, reproducible turbidity.
3. **Why dilute HCl?** To stop other barium salts precipitating.
4. **What is the difference between opalescence and turbidity?** Opalescence is a faint milky appearance (chloride test); turbidity is a heavier cloudiness (sulphate test).
5. **Name a source of sulphate impurity.** Sulphuric acid used in manufacture.
practicals.title: Limit test for sulphates

practicals.markdown:
# Limit test for iron

**Aim:** To perform the limit test for iron on the given sample as per the Indian Pharmacopoeia.

> Iron-free reagents must be used. Follow the monograph quantities and your teacher's instructions.

## Principle

Iron (ferric or ferrous) is reduced to the ferrous state by **thioglycollic acid**. In a solution made alkaline with ammonia and containing citric acid, ferrous iron forms **ferrous thioglycollate**, which is pale pink to deep reddish-purple. The colour is compared with that of a standard prepared from a known quantity of iron.

Fe³⁺ → (thioglycollic acid) → Fe²⁺ → ferrous thioglycollate (purple, in alkaline medium)

| Reagent | Role |
| --- | --- |
| Citric acid (20% w/v, iron-free) | Complexes iron; prevents precipitation as Fe(OH)3 in alkali |
| Thioglycollic acid | Reducing agent and colour-forming reagent |
| Iron-free ammonia | Makes the medium alkaline; colour appears only in alkali |

## Requirements

Nessler cylinders, 20% w/v iron-free citric acid, thioglycollic acid, iron-free ammonia solution, standard iron solution (from ferric ammonium sulphate, 20 µg Fe per ml), distilled water.

## Procedure

| Step | Test | Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Dissolve specified quantity of sample in 40 ml water | 2 ml standard iron solution diluted with 40 ml water |
| 2 | Add 2 ml citric acid solution | Same |
| 3 | Add 0.1 ml thioglycollic acid, mix | Same |
| 4 | Make alkaline with iron-free ammonia; dilute to 50 ml | Same |
| 5 | Allow to stand 5 minutes | Same |

6. Compare the colours by viewing down the cylinders against a white background.

## Observation

Purple colour in test is lighter / deeper than standard.

## Result

The given sample **passes / fails** the limit test for iron.

## Precautions

1. Use iron-free reagents and glassware (no rusty stands or spatulas).
2. Thioglycollic acid has an unpleasant smell; use in a fume hood.
3. Make both solutions alkaline to the same extent.
4. Compare against a white background.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is citric acid added?** To prevent precipitation of iron as hydroxide when ammonia is added.
2. **Why thioglycollic acid?** It reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ and forms the coloured complex.
3. **Why must the solution be alkaline?** Ferrous thioglycollate colour develops only in alkaline medium.
4. **What is the colour of the complex?** Pale pink to reddish-purple.
5. **Source of iron impurity?** Iron vessels and equipment, raw materials.
practicals.title: Limit test for iron

practicals.markdown:
# Limit test for heavy metals

**Aim:** To perform the limit test for heavy metals on the given sample as per the Indian Pharmacopoeia (Method A).

> Method A is for substances that give a clear, colourless solution in water. Other methods in the IP destroy organic matter first. Follow the monograph and your teacher.

## Principle

Heavy metals (lead, copper, mercury, bismuth, antimony, tin, cadmium, silver) react with **hydrogen sulphide** (or sodium sulphide / thioacetamide reagent in newer editions) in a weakly acidic medium (**pH 3–4**) to form **brown to black colloidal metal sulphides**. The colour is compared with a standard lead solution; the limit is expressed in **ppm of lead**.

Pb²⁺ + H2S → PbS (brown–black) + 2H⁺

At pH 3–4 the heavy metal sulphides give a uniform colour, while iron and similar metals do not precipitate.

## Requirements

Nessler cylinders, dilute acetic acid, dilute ammonia, acetate buffer pH 3.5, freshly prepared hydrogen sulphide solution (or sulphide reagent), standard lead solution (from lead nitrate), distilled water, pH paper.

## Procedure

| Step | Test | Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Solution of specified quantity of sample in about 25 ml water | Specified volume of standard lead solution diluted to about 25 ml |
| 2 | Adjust to pH 3–4 with dilute acetic acid or dilute ammonia; add acetate buffer | Same |
| 3 | Dilute to 35 ml with water | Same |
| 4 | Add 10 ml freshly prepared H2S solution | Same |
| 5 | Dilute to 50 ml, stand 5 minutes | Same |

6. View down the cylinders against a white background and compare the brown colour.

## Observation

Colour in test is lighter / darker than standard.

## Result

The given sample **passes / fails** the limit test for heavy metals.

## Precautions

1. Hydrogen sulphide is toxic with a rotten-egg smell: work in a fume hood.
2. Check pH with paper; wrong pH gives wrong colours.
3. Use freshly prepared sulphide reagent.
4. Treat test and standard together and identically.

## Viva questions

1. **Name some heavy metals.** Lead, copper, mercury, bismuth, cadmium, antimony, tin.
2. **Why is pH kept at 3–4?** To get uniform colloidal sulphides and avoid interference by iron.
3. **How is the limit expressed?** In parts per million of lead.
4. **Why are heavy metals dangerous?** They are toxic and accumulate in the body.
5. **What replaces H2S in newer methods?** Sodium sulphide or thioacetamide reagent.
practicals.title: Limit test for heavy metals

practicals.markdown:
# Identification tests for anions and cations (IP)

**Aim:** To identify the anion and cation present in the given inorganic salt using the identification tests of the Indian Pharmacopoeia.

> Use small amounts (a few mg to 0.1 g) and test tubes. Follow your teacher where tests differ.

## Principle

Each ion gives a characteristic reaction (precipitate, colour, gas or flame colour) with specific reagents. The IP lists these "tests for identification" in its appendix and refers to them in monographs.

## Requirements

Test tubes, burner, platinum or nichrome wire, dilute and concentrated acids, ammonia, silver nitrate, barium chloride, ammonium oxalate, ammonium molybdate, potassium ferrocyanide, potassium ferricyanide, ammonium thiocyanate, ferrous sulphate, disodium hydrogen phosphate, sodium cobaltinitrite, lime water, magnesium sulphate.

## Tests for anions

| Anion | Test | Observation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chloride | Solution + dilute HNO3 + AgNO3 | White curdy ppt, soluble in dilute ammonia |
| Bromide | Same | Pale yellow ppt, sparingly soluble in ammonia |
| Iodide | Same | Yellow ppt, insoluble in ammonia |
| Sulphate | Solution + dilute HCl + BaCl2 | White ppt insoluble in HCl |
| Carbonate | Solid + dilute HCl | Effervescence; gas turns lime water milky |
| Bicarbonate | Solution + MgSO4 | No ppt in cold; white ppt on boiling |
| Phosphate | Solution + HNO3 + ammonium molybdate, warm | Yellow crystalline ppt |
| Nitrate | Solution + FeSO4 + conc. H2SO4 poured along the side | Brown ring at the junction |
| Acetate | Solid + H2SO4 + ethanol, warm | Fruity smell of ethyl acetate |

## Tests for cations

| Cation | Test | Observation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sodium | Flame test | Persistent golden yellow flame |
| Potassium | Flame test; solution + sodium cobaltinitrite (acetic acid) | Lilac flame (through blue glass); yellow ppt |
| Calcium | Flame test; solution + ammonium oxalate | Brick-red flame; white ppt insoluble in acetic acid, soluble in HCl |
| Magnesium | Solution + NH4Cl + NH3 + disodium hydrogen phosphate | White crystalline ppt |
| Ferrous iron | Potassium ferricyanide | Dark blue ppt |
| Ferric iron | Potassium ferrocyanide; ammonium thiocyanate | Prussian blue ppt; blood-red colour |
| Ammonium | Warm with NaOH | Smell of ammonia; moist red litmus turns blue |
| Zinc | NaOH dropwise | White ppt soluble in excess |
| Aluminium | NaOH dropwise | White gelatinous ppt soluble in excess |

## Observation table (record)

| Experiment | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| e.g. Flame test | Brick red | Calcium may be present |
| Confirmatory test | ... | ... |

## Result

The given salt contains the ____ cation and the ____ anion.

## Precautions

1. Clean the flame-test wire by dipping in conc. HCl and heating until no colour.
2. Add reagents dropwise; note colours immediately.
3. Use a fume hood for tests that release gases.
4. Do not taste or smell chemicals directly; waft gently.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is the silver chloride ppt dissolved in ammonia?** AgCl forms the soluble diammine silver complex, distinguishing chloride from iodide.
2. **What is the brown ring?** The nitroso-ferrous sulphate complex formed in the nitrate test.
3. **Why view potassium flame through blue glass?** It absorbs the yellow of any sodium present.
4. **Prussian blue is formed by?** Ferric ion with potassium ferrocyanide.
5. **Which cation gives a brick-red flame?** Calcium.
practicals.title: Identification tests for anions and cations (IP)

practicals.markdown:
# Preparation and standardisation of 0.1 N NaOH and 0.1 N KMnO4

**Aim:** (a) To prepare and standardise 0.1 N sodium hydroxide using oxalic acid. (b) To prepare and standardise 0.1 N potassium permanganate using oxalic acid.

> NaOH and KMnO4 are secondary standards: they cannot be weighed exactly, so their exact strength is found against a primary standard. Wear goggles; NaOH is caustic.

## Principle

**(a) NaOH vs oxalic acid (acid–base):**
H2C2O4 + 2NaOH → Na2C2O4 + 2H2O. Indicator: phenolphthalein (colourless → pale pink), because oxalic acid is a weak acid titrated with a strong base.

**(b) KMnO4 vs oxalic acid (redox):**
2MnO4⁻ + 5C2O4²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO2 + 8H2O. Done hot (60–70 °C) in dilute H2SO4. KMnO4 is its own indicator (first permanent faint pink).

## Requirements

NaOH pellets, KMnO4 crystals, oxalic acid dihydrate (AR), dilute H2SO4, phenolphthalein, CO2-free distilled water, volumetric flasks (1 L, 100 ml), burette, pipette, conical flasks, water bath, thermometer, glass wool.

## Preparation of solutions

1. **0.1 N oxalic acid (primary standard):** equivalent weight 63.03; weigh exactly about 0.63 g, dissolve and make up to 100 ml in a volumetric flask. Calculate exact normality from the weight.
2. **0.1 N NaOH:** dissolve about 4.2 g NaOH in CO2-free water and dilute to 1 L.
3. **0.1 N KMnO4:** equivalent weight 31.6 (MW 158.03 ÷ 5); dissolve about 3.2 g in 1 L water, boil 15 minutes, keep 2 days in the dark, filter through glass wool (not paper) and store in an amber bottle.

## Procedure

**(a) NaOH:** Pipette 10 ml oxalic acid into a conical flask, add 2 drops phenolphthalein, titrate with NaOH from the burette to a faint permanent pink. Repeat for three concordant readings.

**(b) KMnO4:** Pipette 10 ml oxalic acid, add about 10 ml dilute H2SO4, warm to 60–70 °C, titrate with KMnO4 (burette, read upper meniscus) until a faint pink lasts 30 seconds. Repeat.

## Observations and calculation

| Titration | Initial (ml) | Final (ml) | Volume used (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.0 | 10.2 | 10.2 |
| 2 | 10.2 | 20.3 | 10.1 |
| 3 | 20.3 | 30.4 | 10.1 |

N1V1 = N2V2 → N(NaOH or KMnO4) = (N oxalic acid × 10) ÷ concordant volume.

Example: 0.1002 × 10 ÷ 10.1 = 0.0992 N.

## Result

Normality of NaOH = ____ N. Normality of KMnO4 = ____ N.

## Precautions

1. Use CO2-free water for NaOH; keep the bottle closed (absorbs CO2).
2. Do not filter KMnO4 through paper (reduces it to MnO2).
3. Heat oxalic acid to 60–70 °C, not boiling.
4. Read the upper meniscus for coloured KMnO4.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is NaOH not a primary standard?** It is hygroscopic and absorbs CO2.
2. **Why is the KMnO4 titration done hot?** The reaction is slow at room temperature; heat (and the Mn²⁺ formed, which catalyses it) speeds it up.
3. **Why H2SO4 and not HCl?** Permanganate oxidises chloride.
4. **What is the equivalent weight of KMnO4 in acid?** 31.6.
5. **Why is the KMnO4 solution boiled and kept?** To oxidise organic matter in the water and settle MnO2, which would otherwise decompose the solution.
practicals.title: Preparation and standardisation of 0.1 N NaOH and 0.1 N KMnO4

practicals.markdown:
# Assay of ferrous sulphate (redox titration)

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of the given ferrous sulphate by titration with standard 0.1 N potassium permanganate.

> The current IP uses 0.1 M ceric ammonium sulphate with ferroin indicator; the KMnO4 method below has the same factor and is widely used in teaching labs. Follow your manual.

## Principle

In acid solution ferrous ions are oxidised to ferric ions by permanganate:

MnO4⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H2O

KMnO4 acts as its own indicator. The equivalent weight of FeSO4·7H2O is its molecular weight, 278.0 (one electron per Fe).

**Factor:** each ml of 0.1 N KMnO4 ≡ 0.02780 g of FeSO4·7H2O.

## Requirements

Ferrous sulphate sample, standardised 0.1 N KMnO4, 1 M (dilute) H2SO4, freshly boiled and cooled water, burette, conical flask, balance.

## Procedure

1. Weigh accurately about 1 g of ferrous sulphate (W).
2. Dissolve in a mixture of about 20 ml dilute H2SO4 and 80 ml freshly boiled and cooled water (removes dissolved oxygen that would oxidise Fe²⁺).
3. Titrate at once with 0.1 N KMnO4 until a faint permanent pink appears.
4. Repeat for concordant readings.

## Observations

| No. | Weight of sample (g) | Burette reading (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1.002 | 35.6 |
| 2 | 1.000 | 35.5 |

## Calculation

% purity = (V × 0.02780 × actual N ÷ 0.1 × 100) ÷ W

Example: V = 35.5 ml, N = 0.1, W = 1.000 g → 35.5 × 0.02780 × 100 ÷ 1.000 = 98.7%.

## Result

The given sample contains ____% w/w of FeSO4·7H2O. (IP requirement for ferrous sulphate is close to 100%; check the monograph limits.)

## Precautions

1. Titrate immediately; Fe²⁺ is oxidised by air.
2. Use freshly boiled and cooled water.
3. Acidify with H2SO4 only.
4. Read the upper meniscus.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is boiled and cooled water used?** To remove dissolved oxygen.
2. **What is the indicator?** KMnO4 itself (self-indicator).
3. **Why does old ferrous sulphate give low results?** Part has oxidised to ferric sulphate.
4. **What is the equivalent weight of ferrous sulphate here?** 278.0 (equal to its molecular weight).
5. **Which indicator is used with ceric ammonium sulphate?** Ferroin (o-phenanthroline ferrous complex).
practicals.title: Assay of ferrous sulphate (redox titration)

practicals.markdown:
# Assay of calcium gluconate (complexometric titration)

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of the given calcium gluconate by complexometric titration with 0.05 M disodium edetate.

> Follow the monograph in your IP edition; the method below is the classical replacement titration.

## Principle

Calcium forms a stable 1 : 1 complex with EDTA at pH 10. Mordant black II (Eriochrome black T) gives a poor end point with calcium alone, so a known volume of **magnesium sulphate** is added. At the end point EDTA removes the last magnesium from the Mg–indicator complex and the colour changes from **wine red to blue**. The volume of MgSO4 added is subtracted.

Ca²⁺ + H2Y²⁻ → CaY²⁻ + 2H⁺ (buffer neutralises the H⁺)

**Factor:** each ml of 0.05 M disodium edetate ≡ 0.02242 g of calcium gluconate (C12H22CaO14·H2O, MW 448.4).

## Requirements

Calcium gluconate, 0.05 M disodium edetate (standardised), 0.05 M magnesium sulphate, strong ammonia–ammonium chloride buffer (pH 10), mordant black II mixture, burette, conical flask, water bath.

## Procedure

1. Weigh accurately about 0.5 g sample (W); dissolve in 50 ml warm water and cool.
2. Add 5.0 ml of 0.05 M MgSO4 and 10 ml ammonia–ammonium chloride buffer.
3. Add a small quantity (about 0.1 g) of mordant black II mixture – wine red colour.
4. Titrate with 0.05 M disodium edetate until the colour changes to blue.
5. Subtract 5.0 ml (volume of MgSO4 added, since both are 0.05 M) from the burette reading.

## Observations and calculation

| Burette reading (ml) | Corrected volume V = reading − 5.0 (ml) |
| --- | --- |
| 27.2 | 22.2 |

% purity = (V × 0.02242 × M ÷ 0.05 × 100) ÷ W

Example: V = 22.2, M = 0.05, W = 0.500 → 22.2 × 0.02242 × 100 ÷ 0.500 = 99.5%.

## Result

The given sample contains ____% of calcium gluconate.

## Precautions

1. Maintain pH 10 with buffer; the indicator works only at this pH.
2. Use metal-free distilled water.
3. Add indicator in small amount; excess gives a dull end point.
4. Titrate slowly near the end point; the change is gradual.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is MgSO4 added?** Mordant black II gives a sharper end point with magnesium (replacement titration).
2. **In what ratio does EDTA bind metals?** 1 : 1.
3. **Why is buffer needed?** H⁺ is released during complexation; the indicator needs pH 10.
4. **Name another indicator for calcium.** Calcon or murexide (hydroxynaphthol blue).
5. **Use of calcium gluconate?** Calcium supplement; IV in hypocalcaemic tetany and hyperkalaemia.
practicals.title: Assay of calcium gluconate (complexometric titration)

practicals.markdown:
# Assay of sodium chloride (modified Volhard's method)

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of the given sodium chloride by the modified Volhard's method.

> Quantities below are typical for a teaching lab. Nitrobenzene is toxic; dibutyl phthalate is a safer alternative. Work in a ventilated area.

## Principle

This is a **back (residual) titration** in nitric acid medium. A known excess of standard silver nitrate precipitates all chloride as AgCl. The unreacted silver nitrate is titrated with standard ammonium thiocyanate using **ferric ammonium sulphate** as indicator; the first excess thiocyanate gives a **reddish-brown** ferric thiocyanate colour.

NaCl + AgNO3 (excess) → AgCl↓ + NaNO3
AgNO3 (remaining) + NH4SCN → AgSCN↓ + NH4NO3
Fe³⁺ + SCN⁻ → [Fe(SCN)]²⁺ (red)

AgCl is more soluble than AgSCN, so near the end point it would react with thiocyanate. **Nitrobenzene (or dibutyl phthalate)** is added to coat the AgCl particles and stop this – hence "modified".

**Factor:** each ml of 0.1 M AgNO3 ≡ 0.005844 g of NaCl.

## Requirements

Sodium chloride, 0.1 M silver nitrate, 0.1 M ammonium thiocyanate (both standardised), dilute nitric acid, nitrobenzene or dibutyl phthalate, ferric ammonium sulphate solution, stoppered conical flask, burettes, pipette.

## Procedure

1. Weigh accurately about 0.1 g NaCl (W); dissolve in about 50 ml water in a stoppered flask.
2. Add 5 ml dilute nitric acid and exactly 50.0 ml of 0.1 M AgNO3.
3. Add 2 ml nitrobenzene (or dibutyl phthalate); stopper and shake well to coagulate the precipitate.
4. Add 2 ml ferric ammonium sulphate solution.
5. Titrate the excess AgNO3 with 0.1 M NH4SCN to a permanent reddish-brown colour (V2 ml).
6. Perform a **blank** with 50.0 ml AgNO3 and the same reagents, without sample (V1 ml).

## Calculation

Volume of AgNO3 used by NaCl (as 0.1 M) = V1 − V2 (ml of 0.1 M thiocyanate equivalent)

% purity = ((V1 − V2) × 0.005844 × 100) ÷ W (correct for actual molarity)

Example: V1 = 50.0, V2 = 33.0, W = 0.1000 g → 17.0 × 0.005844 × 100 ÷ 0.1000 = 99.3%.

## Result

The given sample contains ____% of NaCl.

## Precautions

1. Shake vigorously after adding nitrobenzene so AgCl is fully coated.
2. Keep the solution acidic with nitric acid (iron indicator precipitates in neutral solution).
3. Protect from bright light.
4. Measure 50.0 ml AgNO3 with a pipette or burette accurately.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is this called a back titration?** Excess AgNO3 is added and the excess is titrated.
2. **Role of nitrobenzene?** Coats AgCl to prevent its reaction with thiocyanate.
3. **Why can Mohr's method not be done in acid?** Chromate changes to dichromate and silver chromate dissolves.
4. **What is the indicator?** Ferric ammonium sulphate (ferric alum).
5. **Why is a blank done?** To find the exact volume of AgNO3 used by the sample.
practicals.title: Assay of sodium chloride (modified Volhard's method)

practicals.markdown:
# Assay of ascorbic acid (iodometry / iodimetry)

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of the given ascorbic acid by titration with 0.05 M iodine.

> This is a direct titration with iodine (iodimetry); the syllabus lists it as iodometry. Titrate quickly because ascorbic acid is oxidised by air.

## Principle

Ascorbic acid is a reducing agent. Iodine oxidises it to dehydroascorbic acid; the first excess iodine gives a **blue colour with starch**.

C6H8O6 + I2 → C6H6O6 + 2HI

One mole of ascorbic acid (176.1 g) reacts with one mole of iodine.

**Factor:** each ml of 0.05 M iodine ≡ 0.008806 g of C6H8O6.

## Requirements

Ascorbic acid, 0.05 M iodine (standardised against sodium thiosulphate), 1 M sulphuric acid, starch solution, freshly boiled and cooled water, burette, conical flask.

## Procedure

1. Weigh accurately about 0.1 g ascorbic acid (W).
2. Dissolve in a mixture of 100 ml freshly boiled and cooled water and 25 ml 1 M H2SO4.
3. Titrate **immediately** with 0.05 M iodine, adding 1 ml starch solution near the end point (when the yellow colour of iodine persists faintly).
4. Continue until a permanent **blue** colour appears.
5. Repeat for concordant readings.

## Observations and calculation

| No. | Weight (g) | Volume of 0.05 M iodine (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.1002 | 11.3 |

% purity = (V × 0.008806 × M ÷ 0.05 × 100) ÷ W

Example: 11.3 × 0.008806 × 100 ÷ 0.1002 = 99.3%.

## Result

The given sample contains ____% of ascorbic acid.

## Precautions

1. Use freshly boiled and cooled water (dissolved oxygen oxidises ascorbic acid).
2. Titrate immediately after dissolving.
3. Keep iodine in amber bottles; iodine is volatile.
4. Acid medium slows air oxidation of ascorbic acid.

## Viva questions

1. **Difference between iodimetry and iodometry?** Iodimetry is direct titration with iodine; iodometry titrates liberated iodine with thiosulphate.
2. **Indicator used?** Starch (blue with iodine).
3. **Why is sulphuric acid added?** Ascorbic acid is more stable to air oxidation in acid.
4. **How is iodine solution prepared?** Iodine dissolved in potassium iodide solution (forms soluble KI3).
5. **Use of ascorbic acid?** Scurvy, antioxidant, enhances iron absorption.
practicals.title: Assay of ascorbic acid (iodometry)

practicals.markdown:
# Assay of ibuprofen (alkalimetry)

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of the given ibuprofen by titration with 0.1 M sodium hydroxide.

> Ibuprofen is insoluble in water, so it is dissolved in ethanol. Follow your IP edition.

## Principle

Ibuprofen is a carboxylic acid (2-(4-isobutylphenyl)propanoic acid). It is titrated directly with standard NaOH using phenolphthalein. The ethanol is neutralised to phenolphthalein first so that only the drug uses alkali.

C12H17–COOH + NaOH → C12H17–COONa + H2O

**Factor:** each ml of 0.1 M NaOH ≡ 0.02063 g of C13H18O2 (MW 206.3).

## Requirements

Ibuprofen, 95% ethanol, phenolphthalein, standardised 0.1 M NaOH, burette, conical flask, balance.

## Procedure

1. Neutralise 100 ml ethanol (95%) by adding phenolphthalein and NaOH dropwise to a faint pink.
2. Weigh accurately about 0.5 g ibuprofen (W) and dissolve in the neutralised ethanol.
3. Titrate with 0.1 M NaOH to a faint pink lasting 30 seconds.
4. Repeat for concordant readings.

## Observations and calculation

| No. | Weight (g) | Volume of 0.1 M NaOH (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.5010 | 24.1 |

% purity = (V × 0.02063 × M ÷ 0.1 × 100) ÷ W

Example: 24.1 × 0.02063 × 100 ÷ 0.5010 = 99.2%.

## Result

The given sample contains ____% of ibuprofen.

## Precautions

1. Neutralise the ethanol before adding the sample.
2. Avoid CO2 absorption; titrate promptly and use CO2-free NaOH.
3. Ensure the sample is fully dissolved.
4. Take the first permanent faint pink as end point.

## Viva questions

1. **Why ethanol and not water?** Ibuprofen is practically insoluble in water.
2. **Why phenolphthalein?** Weak acid–strong base titration; equivalence point above pH 7.
3. **Why neutralise the ethanol?** Ethanol may contain traces of acid that would consume NaOH.
4. **What is the active isomer of ibuprofen?** The S-(+) isomer.
5. **Class of ibuprofen?** Propionic acid NSAID.
practicals.title: Assay of ibuprofen (alkalimetry)

practicals.markdown:
# Melting point and boiling point of organic compounds

**Aim:** (a) To determine the melting point of the given organic solid (e.g. benzoic acid, acetanilide) by the capillary method. (b) To determine the boiling point of the given organic liquid by the capillary (Siwoloboff) method.

## Principle

**Melting point** is the temperature at which a solid changes into liquid at atmospheric pressure. A pure compound melts sharply over 0.5–1 °C; impurities **lower** the melting point and **widen** the range. It is used to identify a compound and check its purity. A **mixed melting point** with an authentic sample confirms identity (no depression if the two are the same).

**Boiling point** is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid equals the atmospheric pressure. Pure liquids boil at a constant temperature.

## Requirements

Thiele tube or melting point apparatus, liquid paraffin (heating bath), thermometer (0–250 °C), capillary tubes (one end sealed), small fusion tube, rubber band or thread, burner, porous tile, mortar and pestle.

## Procedure

**(a) Melting point**

1. Powder the dry sample finely; fill a capillary sealed at one end to a height of 2–3 mm by tapping.
2. Tie the capillary to the thermometer so the sample is beside the mercury bulb.
3. Place in the Thiele tube filled with liquid paraffin; heat the side arm gently.
4. Heat quickly to about 10 °C below the expected melting point, then slowly (1–2 °C per minute).
5. Record the temperature when the solid starts to melt (t1) and when it is completely liquid (t2).

**(b) Boiling point**

1. Put a few drops of liquid in a small fusion tube; place inside it a capillary sealed at the upper end, open end down.
2. Tie to the thermometer and heat in the bath.
3. Bubbles escape slowly, then a rapid continuous stream appears; stop heating.
4. Note the temperature at which bubbling stops and the liquid just enters the capillary – this is the boiling point.

## Observations

| Compound | t1 (°C) | t2 (°C) | Range | Literature value (°C) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Benzoic acid | 121 | 122 | 1 °C | about 122 |
| Acetanilide | 113 | 114 | 1 °C | about 114 |

## Result

Melting point of the given solid = ____ °C. Boiling point of the given liquid = ____ °C.

## Precautions

1. Sample must be dry and finely powdered.
2. Heat slowly near the melting point.
3. Thermometer bulb and sample must be at the same level.
4. Stir or use a Thiele tube for uniform heating; do not overheat paraffin.

## Viva questions

1. **Effect of impurity on melting point?** Lowers it and broadens the range.
2. **What is mixed melting point?** Melting point of a mixture with an authentic sample; no depression means same compound.
3. **Why liquid paraffin as bath?** High boiling point, non-volatile, safe to about 250 °C.
4. **Effect of pressure on boiling point?** Higher pressure raises it; lower pressure lowers it.
5. **Why is the Thiele tube shaped so?** Convection currents in the side arm give uniform heating.
practicals.title: Melting point and boiling point of organic compounds

practicals.markdown:
# Preparation of benzoic acid from benzamide

**Aim:** To prepare benzoic acid from benzamide by alkaline hydrolysis and report the practical yield and melting point.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Wear goggles; hot alkali is corrosive.

## Principle

Amides are hydrolysed by boiling with aqueous alkali. Benzamide gives sodium benzoate and ammonia (detected by smell or moist red litmus). Acidifying with HCl liberates **benzoic acid**, which is sparingly soluble in cold water and precipitates.

C6H5CONH2 + NaOH → C6H5COONa + NH3↑
C6H5COONa + HCl → C6H5COOH↓ + NaCl

## Requirements

Benzamide 2 g, 10% w/v NaOH 30 ml, concentrated HCl, round-bottom flask with reflux condenser, heating mantle or water bath, beaker, Buchner funnel, filter paper, litmus paper, ice.

## Procedure

1. Place 2 g benzamide and 30 ml 10% NaOH in a round-bottom flask with a few porcelain pieces.
2. Reflux for 30–40 minutes until no more ammonia is evolved (moist red litmus held at the condenser top no longer turns blue).
3. Cool the flask; transfer the solution to a beaker kept in ice.
4. Add concentrated HCl dropwise with stirring until the solution is acidic to Congo red/litmus; white benzoic acid separates.
5. Filter on a Buchner funnel, wash with a little cold water.
6. Recrystallise from hot water; dry and weigh. Determine the melting point.

## Calculation of yield

C6H5CONH2 (MW 121.1) → C6H5COOH (MW 122.1)

Theoretical yield from 2 g = 2 × 122.1 ÷ 121.1 = 2.02 g

% yield = (practical yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100

Example: practical yield 1.60 g → 1.60 ÷ 2.02 × 100 = 79%.

## Result

Practical yield of benzoic acid = ____ g (____%). Melting point = ____ °C (literature about 122 °C).

## Precautions

1. Reflux until ammonia evolution stops (complete hydrolysis).
2. Acidify in cold, slowly, with stirring.
3. Use minimum hot water for recrystallisation.
4. Dry the product completely before weighing.

## Viva questions

1. **What type of reaction is this?** Alkaline hydrolysis of an amide.
2. **Which gas is evolved?** Ammonia.
3. **Why acidify?** To convert soluble sodium benzoate into insoluble benzoic acid.
4. **Why recrystallise from water?** Benzoic acid is much more soluble in hot than cold water.
5. **Uses of benzoic acid?** Preservative (as sodium benzoate), antifungal in Whitfield's ointment.
practicals.title: Preparation of benzoic acid from benzamide

practicals.markdown:
# Preparation of picric acid from phenol

**Aim:** To prepare picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) from phenol and report the yield and melting point.

> **Safety first.** Dry picric acid is explosive and forms shock-sensitive metal picrates. Keep the product moist, never grind it dry, avoid metal spatulas, and prepare only small amounts. Phenol burns skin. Concentrated acids react violently: use a fume hood, goggles and gloves. Follow your teacher's quantities.

## Principle

Direct nitration of phenol with concentrated nitric acid oxidises it to tar. So phenol is first **sulphonated** with concentrated sulphuric acid to phenol-2,4-disulphonic acid. Then concentrated nitric acid replaces the sulphonic acid groups with nitro groups and nitrates the remaining ortho position, giving picric acid.

C6H5OH + 2H2SO4 → C6H3(OH)(SO3H)2 + 2H2O
C6H3(OH)(SO3H)2 + 3HNO3 → C6H2(OH)(NO2)3 + 2H2SO4 + H2O

## Requirements

Phenol 2 g, concentrated H2SO4 (about 4 ml), concentrated HNO3 (about 7 ml), round-bottom or conical flask, water bath, dropping funnel, beaker of ice water, Buchner funnel.

## Procedure

1. Place 2 g phenol in a dry flask, add 4 ml concentrated H2SO4 and heat on a boiling water bath for about 30 minutes (sulphonation).
2. Cool the flask in ice water.
3. In a fume hood, add 7 ml concentrated HNO3 **dropwise** with shaking; a vigorous reaction with brown fumes occurs.
4. When the reaction slows, heat on the water bath for 1–1.5 hours with occasional shaking.
5. Cool, add about 20 ml cold water; yellow crystals separate.
6. Filter, wash with cold water, and recrystallise from hot dilute acid/water if directed. Keep the product moist.
7. Take a small, dry portion only for melting point.

## Calculation

C6H5OH (MW 94.1) → C6H3N3O7 (MW 229.1)

Theoretical yield from 2 g = 2 × 229.1 ÷ 94.1 = 4.87 g

% yield = practical ÷ theoretical × 100

## Result

Picric acid obtained as yellow crystals; yield ____ g (____%); melting point ____ °C (literature about 122 °C).

## Precautions

1. Never let large amounts of picric acid dry out; store under water.
2. Add nitric acid slowly with cooling.
3. Do all steps in a fume hood (nitrogen oxides are toxic).
4. Avoid contact with metals.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is phenol sulphonated before nitration?** Direct nitration oxidises phenol to tar; sulphonic groups protect the ring and are later replaced by nitro groups.
2. **Why is picric acid strongly acidic?** Three electron-withdrawing nitro groups stabilise the phenoxide ion.
3. **Why is picric acid dangerous?** Dry picric acid and its metal salts are explosive.
4. **Uses of picric acid?** Earlier as an antiseptic for burns; as a reagent (precipitates alkaloids, Jaffe reaction for creatinine).
5. **Colour of picric acid?** Yellow.
practicals.title: Preparation of picric acid from phenol

practicals.markdown:
# Identification and test for purity: aspirin, caffeine, paracetamol, sulfanilamide

**Aim:** To identify the given pharmaceutical substances and perform simple tests for their purity.

> Use small quantities. The pharmacopoeia also uses melting point, IR and TLC; the chemical tests below are the classic ones done in D.Pharm labs.

## Principle

Each drug has a functional group that gives a characteristic reaction (ester, phenol, purine, primary aromatic amine). Purity tests check for known impurities (e.g. free salicylic acid in aspirin, 4-aminophenol in paracetamol) and physical constants such as melting point.

## Requirements

Samples, ferric chloride solution, NaOH, dilute H2SO4, HCl, potassium dichromate solution, potassium chlorate (or hydrogen peroxide), ammonia, sodium nitrite, β-naphthol in NaOH, ethanol, test tubes, water bath, melting point apparatus.

## Tests

### Aspirin

| Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Boil 0.5 g with 10 ml NaOH solution, cool, add excess dilute H2SO4 | White crystalline ppt (salicylic acid), smell of acetic acid | Acetyl ester present |
| Add ferric chloride to the hydrolysed solution | Violet colour | Phenolic –OH of salicylic acid formed |
| Purity: free salicylic acid – dissolve sample in ethanol, add dilute ferric ammonium sulphate | Violet colour not deeper than standard | Limit of free salicylic acid passes |

Unhydrolysed pure aspirin gives no immediate violet colour with ferric chloride.

### Caffeine

| Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Murexide test: evaporate a little caffeine with HCl and a crystal of potassium chlorate (or H2O2) to dryness; expose residue to ammonia vapour | Reddish residue turns purple | Purine (xanthine) nucleus |
| Saturated solution + tannic acid | White ppt soluble in excess reagent | Caffeine (alkaloid) |
| Purity: melting point; loss on drying; sulphated ash | Within limits | Pure |

### Paracetamol

| Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solution + ferric chloride | Blue-violet colour | Phenolic –OH |
| Boil 0.1 g with 1 ml HCl for 3 minutes, add 10 ml water, cool, add a drop of 0.0167 M potassium dichromate | Violet colour slowly develops, not turning red | p-Aminophenol from hydrolysis (indophenol reaction) |
| Purity: limit test for 4-aminophenol; melting point (about 169 °C) | Within limits | Pure |

### Sulfanilamide

| Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dissolve in dilute HCl, cool in ice, add sodium nitrite solution, then pour into alkaline β-naphthol | Orange-red precipitate (azo dye) | Primary aromatic amine |
| Soluble in dilute NaOH and in dilute HCl | Dissolves in both | Amphoteric (acidic sulphonamide + basic amine) |
| Purity: melting point (about 165 °C) | Sharp | Pure |

## Result

The given samples were identified as ____ and found to comply / not comply with the purity tests performed.

## Precautions

1. Use clean test tubes for each test.
2. Diazotisation must be done at 0–5 °C.
3. Evaporate gently in the murexide test; do not char.
4. Compare purity tests with standards prepared the same way.

## Viva questions

1. **Why does aspirin give violet colour only after hydrolysis?** The free phenolic –OH of salicylic acid is needed; in aspirin it is acetylated.
2. **What is the murexide test used for?** Purines such as caffeine and uric acid.
3. **Which impurity is tested in paracetamol?** 4-Aminophenol.
4. **What reaction identifies sulfanilamide?** Diazotisation and coupling with β-naphthol.
5. **Why is ice used in diazotisation?** Diazonium salts decompose above about 5 °C.
practicals.title: Identification and test for purity: aspirin, caffeine, paracetamol, sulfanilamide

practicals.markdown:
# Systematic qualitative analysis of organic compounds

**Aim:** To identify the given organic compound (about 4 substances during the course) by systematic qualitative analysis.

> Typical unknowns: benzoic acid, salicylic acid, phenol, β-naphthol, aniline, acetanilide, benzamide, urea, glucose, acetone, chloroform. Use small amounts.

## Principle

An organic compound is identified step by step: physical characters → ignition test → solubility class → detection of elements (N, S, halogens) by Lassaigne's test → tests for functional groups → melting/boiling point → derivative (if required). Each step narrows the possibilities.

## Requirements

Test tubes, ignition tube, sodium metal (handled with forceps, stored under kerosene), FeSO4, FeCl3, dilute H2SO4, sodium nitroprusside, lead acetate, AgNO3, HNO3, NaOH, NaHCO3, HCl, H2SO4, 2,4-DNP reagent, Schiff's reagent, Tollens' and Fehling's reagents, Molisch reagent, β-naphthol, NaNO2.

## Procedure

**1. Preliminary tests**

| Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| State, colour, odour | e.g. white crystalline, phenolic odour | Possible phenol |
| Ignition on spatula | Sooty smoky flame | Aromatic compound |
| | Non-sooty flame | Aliphatic compound |
| Charring with smell of burnt sugar | | Carbohydrate |

**2. Solubility**

| Solvent | Soluble | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water | Yes | Low-molecular polar compound (urea, glucose, acids, small amines) |
| 5% NaOH, insoluble in water | Yes | Acid or phenol |
| 5% NaHCO3 (with effervescence) | Yes | Carboxylic acid (stronger acid) |
| 5% HCl | Yes | Amine (base) |
| Conc. H2SO4 | Yes | Neutral compound with O or N (ketone, ester, amide) |

**3. Lassaigne's test (sodium fusion):** fuse a little compound with a small piece of sodium in an ignition tube, plunge into water, boil and filter (sodium fusion extract).

| Element | Test on extract | Observation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nitrogen | + FeSO4, boil, cool, add FeCl3 and dilute H2SO4 | Prussian blue colour/ppt |
| Sulphur | + sodium nitroprusside | Violet colour |
| Sulphur | + acetic acid + lead acetate | Black ppt |
| Halogens | Boil with dilute HNO3, add AgNO3 | White (Cl), pale yellow (Br), yellow (I) ppt |

**4. Functional group tests (examples)**

| Group | Test | Positive result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carboxylic acid | NaHCO3 | Brisk effervescence |
| Phenol | Neutral FeCl3 | Violet/green colour |
| Aldehyde | Schiff's reagent; Tollens' | Pink colour; silver mirror |
| Ketone | 2,4-DNP | Yellow-orange ppt; no Tollens' mirror |
| Primary aromatic amine | Diazotisation + β-naphthol | Orange-red dye |
| Amide | Warm with NaOH | Ammonia smell |
| Carbohydrate | Molisch's test | Violet ring |
| Ester | Hydroxamic acid test | Red-violet colour with FeCl3 |

**5. Physical constant:** determine melting point or boiling point and compare with tables.

## Observation table

| Experiment | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ... | ... | ... |

## Result

The given compound is ____ (melting point ____ °C).

## Precautions

1. Handle sodium with forceps; never touch water with it outside the procedure; destroy residues with ethanol.
2. Use small quantities; avoid tasting or direct smelling.
3. Run tests in order; record observations immediately.
4. Use a fume hood for fusion and strong acids.

## Viva questions

1. **What does a sooty flame indicate?** An aromatic (high carbon) compound.
2. **Why is sodium fusion done?** To convert covalently bound N, S and halogens into ionic sodium cyanide, sulphide and halides that can be tested.
3. **How do you distinguish a carboxylic acid from a phenol?** Acids dissolve in NaHCO3 with effervescence; most phenols do not.
4. **Test for aldehyde vs ketone?** Tollens' silver mirror (aldehyde only).
5. **Why must the Lassaigne's extract be boiled with HNO3 before the halogen test?** To decompose cyanide and sulphide which would also precipitate with AgNO3.
practicals.title: Systematic qualitative analysis of organic compounds

questions.answer:
1. Principle: iron is reduced to ferrous state by thioglycollic acid; in ammoniacal solution (citric acid present) it forms ferrous thioglycollate, pale pink to reddish-purple. Colour of sample compared with a standard containing a known amount of iron.
2. Reagents and roles: 20% w/v iron-free citric acid – complexes iron, prevents precipitation as hydroxide in alkali; thioglycollic acid – reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ and forms the coloured complex; iron-free ammonia – makes medium alkaline (colour develops only in alkali).
3. Procedure (test vs standard, Nessler cylinders): sample in 40 ml water / 2 ml standard iron solution (from ferric ammonium sulphate) in 40 ml water; add 2 ml citric acid and 0.1 ml thioglycollic acid to each; make alkaline with ammonia; dilute to 50 ml; stand 5 min.
4. Observation: compare purple colour viewing down the cylinders against white background.
5. Result: sample passes if its colour is not deeper than the standard.
questions.question: Explain the principle and procedure of the limit test for iron. Give the role of each reagent.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: arsenic converted to arsine (AsH3) by nascent hydrogen from arsenic-free Zn + HCl; arsine gives yellow-brown stain on mercuric chloride paper; compared with standard stain from known arsenic.
2. Reactions: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + 2[H]; As(V) reduced to As(III) by KI and SnCl2; H3AsO3 + 6[H] → AsH3 + 3H2O; AsH3 + HgCl2 paper → stain.
3. Roles: KI and stannous chloride reduce As(V) to As(III) and keep evolution even; lead acetate cotton absorbs H2S; mercuric chloride paper detects arsine.
4. Apparatus: wide-mouth bottle with bung, glass tube packed with lead acetate cotton, HgCl2 paper clamped at top between two bungs (draw sketch).
5. Procedure: test solution + KI + SnCl2 + HCl + Zn, close quickly, keep at 40 °C for 40 min; standard done same time. Sample passes if stain not deeper than standard.
questions.question: Describe the Gutzeit test (limit test for arsenic) with a labelled sketch of the apparatus.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: any foreign substance present in a drug other than the drug itself or intended additives.
2. Sources: raw materials (rock salt brings Ca, Mg salts); manufacturing process (reagents, catalysts, solvents, intermediates, side products, arsenic from H2SO4); reaction vessels (Fe, Cu, Pb, alkali from glass); atmosphere (dust, moisture, CO2 – NaOH forms Na2CO3); storage and decomposition (ferrous sulphate oxidises, aspirin hydrolyses, adrenaline turns pink); packaging (leaching from plastics and rubber); physical changes (polymorphs); accidental contamination/adulteration.
3. Effects: toxicity (lead, arsenic – cumulative); reduced potency; instability (metal ions catalyse oxidation); changes in colour, odour, taste, solubility; incompatibility; interference with assays.
4. Control: pharmacopoeial limit tests, good manufacturing practice, proper storage.
questions.question: What are impurities? Discuss the sources and effects of impurities in pharmaceutical substances.

questions.answer: Principle: Cl⁻ + AgNO3 in dilute HNO3 → AgCl opalescence, compared with standard (dilute NaCl). Procedure: sample and standard each in Nessler cylinder with 10 ml dilute HNO3, diluted to 50 ml, 1 ml 0.1 M AgNO3 added, stood 5 min away from light. Sample passes if opalescence is not more than standard. Nitric acid prevents precipitation of other silver salts.
questions.question: Explain the limit test for chlorides.

questions.answer: SO4²⁻ + BaCl2 in dilute HCl → BaSO4 turbidity compared with standard K2SO4 solution; volume 50 ml, stand 5 min. Barium sulphate reagent = BaCl2 + sulphate-free alcohol + a little K2SO4. K2SO4 gives seed crystals so turbidity forms quickly and uniformly; alcohol prevents supersaturation; HCl stops precipitation of barium carbonate/phosphate.
questions.question: Explain the limit test for sulphates. Why is potassium sulphate added to barium sulphate reagent?

questions.answer: Accuracy: closeness of a result to the true value; expressed as error; affected by systematic errors. Precision: closeness of repeated results to each other; expressed as deviation/standard deviation; affected by random errors. Results can be precise but inaccurate (e.g. using an uncalibrated burette repeatedly).
questions.question: Differentiate between accuracy and precision.

questions.answer: Determinate (systematic): instrumental, method, personal, reagent – traceable, one direction. Indeterminate (random): uncontrollable, scatter both ways. Gross: blunders. Minimise by calibration of apparatus, blank and control determinations, independent method, parallel (replicate) determinations, standard addition, internal standard.
questions.question: Classify errors and give methods to minimise them.

questions.answer: Heavy metals (Pb, Cu, Hg, Bi, Sb, Sn, Cd, Ag) react with H2S (or sulphide reagent) at pH 3–4 (acetate buffer) to give brown–black colloidal sulphides. The colour is compared with a standard lead solution under identical conditions; result expressed as ppm of lead. At pH 3–4 interfering metals like iron do not precipitate.
questions.question: Write the principle of the limit test for heavy metals.

questions.answer: A quantitative or semi-quantitative test that checks that a small, permitted amount of a known impurity in a substance is not exceeded, by comparing it with a standard.
questions.question: Define limit test.

questions.answer: All non-zero digits and zeros between them are significant; leading zeros are not; trailing zeros after a decimal point are. Example: 0.02050 has 4 significant figures.
questions.question: Give the rules for counting significant figures with one example.

questions.answer: To absorb hydrogen sulphide formed from sulphide impurities in zinc, which would otherwise darken the mercuric chloride paper and give a false stain.
questions.question: Why is lead acetate cotton used in the Gutzeit test?

questions.answer:
1. Titrations done in solvents other than water for very weak acids/bases or water-insoluble drugs; water competes as weak acid/base and blurs end point.
2. Solvents: aprotic (benzene, chloroform – inert diluents); protophilic (pyridine, DMF, ethylenediamine – enhance acidity, used for weak acids); protogenic (glacial acetic acid, formic acid – enhance basicity, used for weak bases); amphiprotic (water, alcohols).
3. Weak bases: titrant 0.1 M perchloric acid in glacial acetic acid; acetic acid forms onium ion CH3COOH2⁺ which protonates the base; indicator crystal violet (violet → blue-green); standardised with potassium hydrogen phthalate; acetic anhydride removes water.
4. Halide salts (e.g. ephedrine HCl): add mercuric acetate to convert halide to undissociated HgX2, releasing acetate which is titrated.
5. Examples: ephedrine, chlorpromazine HCl, diazepam.
questions.question: What are non-aqueous titrations? Explain the types of solvents and the titration of weak bases with an example.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: metal ion + chelating agent → stable soluble complex. EDTA (disodium edetate) has 6 donor atoms, reacts 1 : 1 with metal regardless of charge; H⁺ released so buffer used (pH 10 ammonia–NH4Cl for Ca, Mg).
2. Metal ion indicators: form weaker coloured complex with metal; at end point EDTA removes metal and free indicator colour shows. Eriochrome black T (mordant black II) wine red → blue (Mg, Zn, pH 10); murexide (Ca, Ni, Cu); calcon/hydroxynaphthol blue (Ca, pH 12–13); xylenol orange (Bi, Pb, Zn in acid).
3. Types: direct (Zn, Mg salts); back titration – excess EDTA, excess titrated with Zn/Mg (Al, Pb); replacement – Mg–EDTA added, analyte displaces Mg (Ca with EBT); indirect – for anions like sulphate, phosphate.
4. Masking with cyanide, triethanolamine, fluoride stops interference.
5. Examples: calcium gluconate, magnesium sulphate, zinc oxide.
questions.question: Explain complexometric titrations. Describe the types and the metal ion indicators used.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: analyte forms sparingly soluble precipitate with titrant; argentometry uses AgNO3 for halides (Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl).
2. Mohr's method: direct titration of chloride with AgNO3 in neutral/faintly alkaline medium (pH 6.5–9); indicator potassium chromate; end point first permanent red-brown Ag2CrO4. Fails in acid.
3. Volhard's method: acidic (HNO3); excess standard AgNO3 added; unreacted Ag⁺ back-titrated with NH4SCN using ferric ammonium sulphate; end point red Fe(SCN)²⁺. Modified Volhard: nitrobenzene/dibutyl phthalate coats AgCl to stop it reacting with thiocyanate.
4. Fajans' method: adsorption indicators (fluorescein, dichlorofluorescein, eosin); after equivalence point the indicator anion adsorbs on the positively charged precipitate and changes colour.
5. Example: assay of NaCl, KCl.
questions.question: Describe precipitation titrations. Explain Mohr's, Volhard's and Fajans' methods.

questions.answer: Iodimetry: direct titration with standard iodine; analyte is a reducing agent (ascorbic acid); end point – blue colour with starch appears. Iodometry: oxidising analyte liberates iodine from KI, which is titrated with sodium thiosulphate (CuSO4, bleaching powder); end point – blue disappears; starch added near the end point.
questions.question: Differentiate between iodimetry and iodometry.

questions.answer: A substance pure enough for a standard solution to be made by direct weighing. Qualities: high purity, stable in air (not hygroscopic, no CO2 absorption), easy to dry and weigh, high equivalent weight, reacts stoichiometrically and fast, soluble. Examples: potassium hydrogen phthalate, anhydrous Na2CO3, oxalic acid, K2Cr2O7, NaCl.
questions.question: Define primary standard. Give its qualities with examples.

questions.answer: Ostwald: indicator is weak acid HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻; HIn and In⁻ differ in colour; acid shifts to HIn colour, alkali to In⁻ colour. Quinonoid theory: indicator exists in benzenoid and quinonoid tautomers of different colour; pH change shifts the balance (phenolphthalein becomes pink quinonoid in alkali).
questions.question: Explain the theory of acid–base indicators.

questions.answer: KMnO4 is a strong oxidant in acid: MnO4⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H2O; acts as its own indicator (first excess drop gives permanent pink). H2SO4 is used because HCl is oxidised by permanganate to chlorine (high results) and HNO3 is itself an oxidant. Example: assay of ferrous sulphate, H2O2.
questions.question: Write the principle of permanganometry. Why is H2SO4 used and not HCl?

questions.answer: Constituent converted to a pure insoluble compound of known composition, which is weighed. Steps: weigh sample, dissolve, precipitate (hot, dilute, slowly), digest, filter, wash, dry/ignite to constant weight, weigh, calculate using gravimetric factor (e.g. sulphate weighed as BaSO4). Errors: co-precipitation, post-precipitation, peptisation.
questions.question: Write the principle and steps of gravimetric analysis.

questions.answer: Phenolphthalein, because the equivalence point is above pH 7 and the steep part of the curve (about pH 7–10) covers its range of 8.3–10.
questions.question: Which indicator is used for titration of a weak acid with a strong base and why?

questions.answer: It converts the halide ion of amine hydrohalide salts into undissociated mercuric halide and releases an equivalent amount of acetate, which can then be titrated with perchloric acid.
questions.question: What is the role of mercuric acetate in non-aqueous titration?

questions.answer:
1. Antacids are weak bases that neutralise gastric HCl and raise gastric pH (hyperacidity, dyspepsia, peptic ulcer).
2. Ideal: fast and long action, not absorbed, no acid rebound, no alkalosis, no CO2, no constipation/diarrhoea, palatable, cheap.
3. Classification: systemic (NaHCO3); non-systemic – Al(OH)3, Mg(OH)2, magaldrate, CaCO3.
4. Aluminium hydroxide gel: Al(OH)3 + 3HCl → AlCl3 + 3H2O; slow, causes constipation, binds phosphate (used as phosphate binder); combined with Mg(OH)2 (Digene, Gelusil); store well-closed, do not freeze.
5. Sodium bicarbonate: NaHCO3 + HCl → NaCl + H2O + CO2; quick, short; belching, alkalosis, sodium load, acid rebound; uses: occasional antacid, metabolic acidosis, urinary alkaliniser; store well-closed.
questions.question: What are antacids? Give their ideal properties and classification. Describe aluminium hydroxide gel and sodium bicarbonate.

questions.answer:
1. Haematinics help form haemoglobin and RBCs; used in iron-deficiency anaemia. Iron absorbed as Fe²⁺ in duodenum; vitamin C helps; antacids, tea, tetracyclines reduce.
2. Ferrous sulphate FeSO4·7H2O: tablets (200 mg dried ≈ 65 mg Fe), with folic acid (Fefol), syrups; oxidises in moist air – airtight container; uses: anaemia, pregnancy supplement.
3. Ferrous fumarate: ~33% Fe, stable, tasteless; tablets/capsules with folic acid, B12 (Livogen); store cool dry.
4. Ferric ammonium citrate: brown scales, deliquescent, light sensitive; syrups for children (Dexorange); airtight, light-resistant containers; ferric form less absorbed.
5. Side effects: GI upset, constipation, black stools; keep away from children (overdose toxic).
questions.question: What are haematinics? Write the formulations, storage and uses of ferrous sulphate, ferrous fumarate and ferric ammonium citrate.

questions.answer:
1. Silver nitrate AgNO3: antiseptic, astringent, caustic; sticks for warts and granulation tissue; stains skin black; store in light-resistant containers.
2. Hydrogen peroxide: 6% w/v (20 volume); releases oxygen with catalase, effervescence cleans wounds; ear wax, mouthwash; decomposes with light/heat/metal – stabiliser added; store cool, dark, vented closure.
3. Potassium permanganate KMnO4: oxidising antiseptic; 1:1,000–1:10,000 solutions for wounds, fungal foot soaks, eczema; stains brown; never apply crystals; keep away from organic matter.
4. Bleaching powder (chlorinated lime, ~CaOCl2): ≥30% available chlorine; releases HOCl; disinfects water, latrines, drains; loses chlorine in air/moisture/light – airtight, cool, dark storage.
questions.question: Write a note on topical agents: silver nitrate, hydrogen peroxide, potassium permanganate and bleaching powder.

questions.answer: Al salts cause constipation and act slowly; Mg salts cause diarrhoea and act quickly – combination balances bowel effect and gives quick plus lasting relief. Magaldrate: hydrated magnesium aluminate (Al-Mg hydroxide sulphate), one compound with both actions; suspension/tablets often with simethicone; used in hyperacidity, gastritis, ulcer.
questions.question: Why are aluminium and magnesium antacids combined? Write about magaldrate.

questions.answer: Oxygen: hypoxia, resuscitation, anaesthesia; cylinder black with white shoulder; no oil/grease. Nitrous oxide: analgesic, weak anaesthetic, Entonox (50% with O2) for labour; blue cylinder. Carbon dioxide: laparoscopic insufflation, dry ice cryotherapy; grey cylinder. Store upright, chained, cool ventilated area, away from heat and flames.
questions.question: Write the uses and storage of medicinal gases.

questions.answer: Sodium fluoride: anticaries – converts hydroxyapatite to acid-resistant fluorapatite; toothpaste, rinses; excess causes fluorosis. Calcium carbonate: abrasive/polishing agent in dentifrices. Denture cleaners: alkaline peroxide effervescent tablets (sodium perborate/percarbonate), hypochlorite, enzymes. Denture adhesives: sodium CMC and PVM/MA copolymer salts that swell and hold dentures.
questions.question: Write a note on dental products: sodium fluoride, calcium carbonate, denture cleaners and denture adhesives.

questions.answer: Cathartics promote bowel evacuation; inorganic ones are saline (osmotic) purgatives that retain water in the gut. Magnesium sulphate (Epsom salt, MgSO4·7H2O): saline purgative in the morning with plenty of water; IV/IM to control convulsions in eclampsia; paste with glycerin for boils; store well-closed, cool (effloresces).
questions.question: What are cathartics? Write about magnesium sulphate.

questions.answer: A solution (about 6% w/v H2O2) of which 1 ml releases about 20 ml of oxygen at normal temperature and pressure.
questions.question: What is meant by 20 volume hydrogen peroxide?

questions.answer: It is used in achlorhydria; sipping it well diluted through a straw prevents the acid from damaging the tooth enamel.
questions.question: Why is dilute HCl taken through a straw?

questions.answer:
1. Heterocycles: cyclic compounds with at least one ring atom other than carbon (N, O, S); present in nucleic acid bases, vitamins, alkaloids and most synthetic drugs.
2. Name = heteroatom prefix + stem for ring size and saturation.
3. Prefixes in priority order: oxa > thia > selena > aza > phospha; 'a' dropped before a vowel.
4. Stems: 3 – irine/iridine (N), irene/irane; 4 – ete/etidine, ete/etane; 5 – ole/olidine, ole/olane; 6 – ine/inane, ine/ane; 7 – epine/epane; 8 – ocine/ocane.
5. Numbering: heteroatom = 1; higher-priority heteroatom first; lowest locants to others; indicated hydrogen (1H-, 2H-).
6. Examples: oxirane (ethylene oxide), aziridine, azetidine (β-lactam ring), 1,3-thiazole, 1,2,4-triazole, 1,3-diazine (pyrimidine), azinane (piperidine), 1,4-oxazinane (morpholine).
questions.question: What are heterocyclic compounds? Explain the Hantzsch–Widman system of nomenclature with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Classification: by ring size (3–8), by number of rings (mono-, bi-, tricyclic fused), by saturation (aromatic, partly saturated, saturated), by heteroatom (N, O, S, mixed).
2. Five-membered: furan (O) – furosemide; thiophene (S) – olanzapine; pyrrole/pyrrolidine (N) – captopril (proline); imidazole – ketoconazole, metronidazole; triazole – fluconazole; thiazolidine – penicillins; hydantoin – phenytoin; isoxazole – sulfamethoxazole.
3. Six-membered: pyridine – isoniazid; pyrimidine – barbiturates, 5-FU; pyrazine – pyrazinamide; piperidine – haloperidol; piperazine – ciprofloxacin; morpholine – linezolid.
4. Draw the ring for each and mark the heteroatom position 1.
questions.question: Classify heterocyclic compounds and give the structures and one drug example for five-membered and six-membered heterocycles.

questions.answer:
1. Bicyclic: indole (benzene + pyrrole) – indomethacin; benzimidazole – albendazole, omeprazole; quinoline – chloroquine, fluoroquinolones; isoquinoline – papaverine; quinazoline – prazosin; purine (pyrimidine + imidazole) – caffeine, acyclovir, mercaptopurine; pteridine – methotrexate; 1,4-benzodiazepine – diazepam; benzisoxazole – risperidone; tropane – atropine; penam – penicillins.
2. Tricyclic: phenothiazine – chlorpromazine; dibenzazepine – imipramine, carbamazepine; acridine – tacrine; carbazole – carvedilol; thioxanthene – flupentixol; dibenzothiazepine – quetiapine.
3. Fusion naming: prefix in 'o' (benzo, pyrido, thieno) + base component + letter for fused bond, e.g. benzo[b]thiophene, triazolo[4,3-a][1,4]benzodiazepine (alprazolam).
questions.question: Name the important fused bicyclic and tricyclic heterocyclic ring systems and give drugs that contain them.

questions.answer: Phenytoin: 5,5-diphenylimidazolidine-2,4-dione – saturated 5-ring with two N, C=O at 2 and 4, two phenyls at 5. Phenobarbital: 5-ethyl-5-phenylpyrimidine-2,4,6(1H,3H,5H)-trione – pyrimidine with three C=O, ethyl and phenyl at 5. Isoniazid: pyridine-4-carbohydrazide – pyridine with –CONHNH2 at position 4.
questions.question: Write the IUPAC names of phenytoin, phenobarbital and isoniazid and explain each name.

questions.answer: Heteroatom gets position 1; with different heteroatoms number from the highest priority (O > S > N) and give others lowest locants; same heteroatoms get lowest set of numbers together; indicated hydrogen (1H, 2H) shows the position of the extra H; substituents then get lowest possible numbers.
questions.question: What are the rules for numbering heterocyclic rings?

questions.answer: Chemical (IUPAC) name describes exact structure: N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide. Generic (non-proprietary) name is the official short name used in pharmacopoeias: paracetamol. Brand (proprietary) name is given by a manufacturer: Crocin, Calpol, Dolo; one generic can have many brands.
questions.question: Differentiate between chemical, generic and brand names of a drug with an example.

questions.answer: Ketoconazole – imidazole (plus piperazine, dioxolane); fluconazole – 1,2,4-triazole; chlorpromazine – phenothiazine; imipramine – dibenzazepine; caffeine – purine (xanthine); ciprofloxacin – quinolone (plus piperazine).
questions.question: Name the heterocyclic ring present in: ketoconazole, fluconazole, chlorpromazine, imipramine, caffeine, ciprofloxacin.

questions.answer: A cyclic compound containing at least one atom other than carbon (N, O or S) in the ring, e.g. pyridine and furan.
questions.question: Define a heterocyclic compound with two examples.

questions.answer: Pyrrole = azole (1H-azole); piperidine = azinane.
questions.question: Give the Hantzsch–Widman names of pyrrole and piperidine.

questions.answer:
1. Classification: typical – phenothiazines (chlorpromazine, fluphenazine), butyrophenones (haloperidol), benzamides (sulpiride); atypical – benzisoxazole (risperidone), thienobenzodiazepine (olanzapine), dibenzothiazepine (quetiapine), benzisothiazole (lurasidone).
2. Chlorpromazine: 3-(2-chloro-10H-phenothiazin-10-yl)-N,N-dimethylpropan-1-amine HCl.
3. Structure: phenothiazine tricyclic with Cl at C-2 and –(CH2)3N(CH3)2 on N-10 (draw); 3-carbon chain needed.
4. Action: D2 blocker. Uses: schizophrenia, mania, antiemetic, hiccups, tetanus, potentiation of anaesthesia.
5. Adverse: sedation, hypotension, EPS, jaundice, photosensitivity.
6. Storage: oxidised by light/air to sulphoxide (pink/yellow) – light-resistant, well-closed; discard discoloured injection. Brand: Largactil.
questions.question: Classify antipsychotic drugs. Give the structure, chemical name, uses and storage of chlorpromazine hydrochloride.

questions.answer:
1. Classification: barbiturates (phenobarbital, thiopental); benzodiazepines (diazepam, alprazolam, nitrazepam); Z-drugs (zolpidem); others (chloral hydrate).
2. Mechanism: GABA-A Cl⁻ channel – BZDs ↑ frequency, barbiturates ↑ duration of opening.
3. Diazepam: 7-chloro-1-methyl-5-phenyl-1,3-dihydro-2H-1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one; benzodiazepine nucleus with 7-Cl, N1-CH3, 5-phenyl (draw). Uses: anxiety, status epilepticus, febrile fits, muscle spasm, alcohol withdrawal, preoperative. Brand: Valium, Calmpose.
4. Phenobarbital: 5-ethyl-5-phenylbarbituric acid; barbituric ring with ethyl and phenyl at C-5 (draw). Uses: anticonvulsant (GTCS, status, febrile), sedative; enzyme inducer. Brand: Gardenal.
5. Storage: well-closed, light protected.
questions.question: Classify sedatives and hypnotics. Write the chemical name, structure and uses of diazepam and phenobarbital.

questions.answer:
1. Classes: barbiturates (phenobarbital), hydantoins (phenytoin), iminostilbenes (carbamazepine), benzodiazepines (clonazepam), fatty acids (valproic acid), GABA analogues (gabapentin, vigabatrin), phenyltriazine (lamotrigine), sulphamate (topiramate).
2. Phenytoin: 5,5-diphenylimidazolidine-2,4-dione (hydantoin ring + two phenyls at C-5); Na channel blocker; uses GTCS, partial, status, trigeminal neuralgia, digitalis arrhythmia; adverse gum hypertrophy, hirsutism, ataxia, nystagmus, megaloblastic anaemia, teratogenic; zero-order kinetics; injection precipitates in dextrose. Brand: Eptoin.
3. Carbamazepine: 5H-dibenzo[b,f]azepine-5-carboxamide (iminostilbene + CONH2); uses partial seizures, trigeminal neuralgia, bipolar; adverse diplopia, hyponatraemia, SJS, blood dyscrasias, autoinduction; keep dry. Brand: Tegretol.
questions.question: Classify anticonvulsants. Write the structure, chemical name, uses and adverse effects of phenytoin and carbamazepine.

questions.answer:
1. Classes: TCAs (imipramine, amitriptyline), SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram, fluvoxamine, paroxetine), SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine), MAOIs (moclobemide), atypical (mirtazapine).
2. Imipramine: dibenzazepine with N in central 7-ring carrying –(CH2)3N(CH3)2; uses depression, nocturnal enuresis.
3. Amitriptyline: dibenzocycloheptene; central ring C joined by double bond (=CH–CH2CH2N(CH3)2); sedating; uses depression with insomnia, neuropathic pain, migraine prophylaxis.
4. TCA adverse: anticholinergic, sedation, hypotension, arrhythmia, toxic in overdose.
5. Fluoxetine: N-methyl-3-phenyl-3-[4-(trifluoromethyl)phenoxy]propan-1-amine; SSRI; long half-life (norfluoxetine); depression, OCD, bulimia; no MAOI combination (serotonin syndrome). Brand: Fludac.
questions.question: Classify antidepressants. Compare the structures and uses of imipramine and amitriptyline and write on fluoxetine.

questions.answer: Ultra-short-acting barbiturate: sodium 5-ethyl-5-(1-methylbutyl)-2-thiobarbiturate (S replaces O at C-2 → high lipid solubility). Rapid onset (one arm–brain time), short action due to redistribution. Uses: induction of anaesthesia, status epilepticus. Solution strongly alkaline and unstable – reconstitute fresh; extravasation causes necrosis.
questions.question: Write a note on thiopental sodium.

questions.answer: 2-propylpentanoic acid: CH3CH2CH2–CH(COOH)–CH2CH2CH3, a branched fatty acid. Broad-spectrum antiepileptic (absence, myoclonic, GTCS, partial), bipolar disorder, migraine prophylaxis. Adverse: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, weight gain, hair loss, teratogenic (neural tube defects). Sodium valproate hygroscopic – airtight storage.
questions.question: Write the chemical name, structure and uses of valproic acid.

questions.answer: 2-(2-chlorophenyl)-2-(methylamino)cyclohexanone HCl. NMDA antagonist – dissociative anaesthesia with strong analgesia, raises BP and heart rate, bronchodilator. Uses: induction in shocked/asthmatic patients, children, short procedures, burns dressing. Adverse: emergence hallucinations, raised ICP; abuse potential.
questions.question: Write a note on ketamine hydrochloride.

questions.answer: Butyrophenone: 4-[4-(4-chlorophenyl)-4-hydroxypiperidin-1-yl]-1-(4-fluorophenyl)butan-1-one – p-fluorophenyl ketone, 3-carbon chain, 4-hydroxy-4-(p-chlorophenyl)piperidine. Potent D2 blocker. Uses: schizophrenia, mania, delirium, Tourette's, antiemetic; decanoate depot. Marked EPS, little sedation.
questions.question: Write the structure and uses of haloperidol.

questions.answer: 2-[1-(aminomethyl)cyclohexyl]acetic acid – GABA built on a cyclohexane ring (lipophilic). Binds α2δ subunit of Ca channels (not GABA receptors).
