# Unit 8: Diuretics

A **diuretic** increases the output of urine by increasing the excretion of **sodium and water** (natriuresis) by the kidney. Diuretics are used in oedema (heart failure, liver cirrhosis, kidney disease), hypertension, glaucoma and some electrolyte disorders. The syllabus lists acetazolamide, frusemide\* (furosemide), bumetanide, chlorthalidone, benzthiazide, metolazone, xipamide and spironolactone.

## 8.1 How the kidney handles sodium (where diuretics act)

```text
   Glomerulus → Proximal tubule → Loop of Henle → Distal tubule → Collecting duct → urine
                 (~65% Na reabsorbed) (thick ascending   (~5–8%)       (~2–3%, aldosterone
                                       limb ~25%)                       controlled)

   Site 1  Proximal tubule ........... carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide)
   Site 2  Thick ascending limb ...... loop diuretics (frusemide, bumetanide)
   Site 3  Early distal tubule ....... thiazides and thiazide-like (benzthiazide,
                                        chlorthalidone, metolazone, xipamide)
   Site 4  Late distal / collecting .. potassium-sparing (spironolactone)
```

**Efficacy** depends on how much sodium normally passes the site: loop diuretics act where a large share is reabsorbed, so they are the most powerful (**high ceiling**).

## 8.2 Classification

| Class | Drugs | Efficacy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **High ceiling (loop) diuretics** | Frusemide, bumetanide, torsemide | High (can excrete up to about 20–25% of filtered Na) |
| **Thiazides and thiazide-like (medium efficacy)** | Benzthiazide, hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, metolazone, xipamide, indapamide | Moderate (5–10%) |
| **Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (weak)** | Acetazolamide | Low |
| **Potassium-sparing (weak)** | Aldosterone antagonist: spironolactone, eplerenone; Na-channel blockers: amiloride, triamterene | Low (2–3%) |
| **Osmotic diuretics** | Mannitol, glycerol | Variable |

Most important diuretics (frusemide, thiazides, acetazolamide) contain a **sulphonamide (–SO2NH2) group**, and some patients allergic to sulphonamides react to them.

## 8.3 Loop (high-ceiling) diuretics

**Mechanism:** inhibit the **Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter** in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Act within minutes when given IV and work even when kidney function is poor.

### Frusemide\* (furosemide)

- **Chemical name:** 4-chloro-2-[(furan-2-ylmethyl)amino]-5-sulfamoylbenzoic acid.
- **Structure:** an **anthranilic acid** (2-aminobenzoic acid) derivative. On the benzene ring: –COOH (1), –NH–CH2–furan (2), Cl (4) and –SO2NH2 (5). The **furfuryl** group gives the name.

```text
   Benzene ring, positions:
     C-1  –COOH                      (benzoic acid)
     C-2  –NH–CH2–(furan-2-yl)       (furfurylamino; with C-1 = anthranilic acid)
     C-4  –Cl
     C-5  –SO2NH2                    (sulphamoyl)
   C-3 and C-6 carry hydrogen.
```

(COOH and the furfurylamino group are next to each other; Cl and the sulphamoyl group are next to each other.)

- **Uses:** **acute pulmonary oedema** (IV, acts quickly also by dilating veins), oedema of heart failure, cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome, oedema with renal failure, hypertension (with renal impairment), hypercalcaemia (with saline), forced diuresis in some poisonings.
- **Adverse effects:** **hypokalaemia** (low potassium) and metabolic alkalosis, hyponatraemia, dehydration and low BP, **hyperuricaemia** (gout), hyperglycaemia, **ototoxicity** (deafness with high IV doses, worse with aminoglycosides), hypomagnesaemia, low calcium.
- **Interactions:** with digoxin (hypokalaemia increases digoxin toxicity), aminoglycosides (ear and kidney damage), lithium (raised levels), NSAIDs (reduce diuretic effect).
- **Stability/storage:** frusemide is **light sensitive** (discolours, degrades). Tablets and injections are stored in **light-resistant containers**; do not use discoloured injection. The injection is alkaline (sodium salt) and should not be mixed with acidic solutions (precipitates).
- **Formulations/brands:** tablets 40 mg, injection 10 mg/ml; Lasix; combinations with spironolactone (Lasilactone) and amiloride.

### Bumetanide

- 3-butylamino-4-phenoxy-5-sulphamoylbenzoic acid (also a sulphamoylbenzoic acid).
- About **40 times more potent** than frusemide on weight basis, similar maximum effect; better oral absorption; less ototoxic.
- Uses: same as frusemide. Brand: Bumet.

## 8.4 Thiazides and thiazide-like diuretics

**Mechanism:** inhibit the **Na⁺–Cl⁻ cotransporter** in the early distal tubule. Effect is moderate and long; they **lose effect when kidney function is poor** (except metolazone).

**Extra effects:** reduce calcium excretion (useful in calcium kidney stones and osteoporosis), mild vasodilation (antihypertensive effect continues after diuresis settles), paradoxical antidiuretic action in **nephrogenic diabetes insipidus**.

**Adverse effects (common to the group):** hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperglycaemia, raised lipids, hypercalcaemia, impotence.

**Basic thiazide structure (benzothiadiazine)**

```text
   Thiazide nucleus = 2H-1,2,4-benzothiadiazine 1,1-dioxide

     benzene ring fused to a six-membered ring containing
     S (as SO2) at 1, N at 2, C at 3, N at 4

     position 6 : –Cl (or –CF3)        position 7 : –SO2NH2
     position 3 : varies (benzthiazide: –CH2–S–CH2–C6H5)
     3,4-dihydro forms (e.g. hydrochlorothiazide) are more potent
```

A **6-chloro** (or CF3) and a **7-sulphamoyl** group on the benzothiadiazine-1,1-dioxide ring are essential.

| Drug | Chemistry | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Benzthiazide** | Benzothiadiazine (thiazide) with a benzylthiomethyl group at position 3 | Oedema, hypertension |
| **Chlorthalidone** | **Phthalimidine** (isoindolinone) with chlorobenzenesulphonamide – "thiazide-like", no thiazide ring | **Long acting (48–72 h)**, once daily; widely used in hypertension; brand: Thalitone |
| **Metolazone** | **Quinazolinone** sulphonamide | Effective even when GFR is low; with frusemide for resistant oedema (powerful combination – watch potassium) |
| **Xipamide** | **Salicylanilide** sulphonamide (4-chloro-5-sulphamoyl salicylic acid amide) | Thiazide-like; oedema and hypertension |

## 8.5 Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors

### Acetazolamide

- **Chemistry:** N-(5-sulfamoyl-1,3,4-thiadiazol-2-yl)acetamide – a **thiadiazole sulphonamide**.
- **Mechanism:** inhibits **carbonic anhydrase** in the proximal tubule → less H⁺ formed for exchange with Na⁺ → bicarbonate, sodium and water lost in alkaline urine. Effect is weak and **self-limiting** (metabolic acidosis develops in 2–3 days).
- **Uses:** **glaucoma** (reduces aqueous humour formation – main use), acute **mountain sickness**, to alkalinise urine, some epilepsies, periodic paralysis.
- **Adverse effects:** metabolic acidosis, hypokalaemia, kidney stones, paraesthesia (tingling), drowsiness, sulphonamide allergy.
- Brand: Diamox (tablets).

## 8.6 Potassium-sparing diuretics

### Spironolactone

- **Chemistry:** a **steroid** (similar to aldosterone) with a **lactone** ring at C-17 and a thioacetyl group at C-7.
- **Mechanism:** **competitive antagonist of aldosterone** at mineralocorticoid receptors in the late distal tubule and collecting duct → Na⁺ lost, **K⁺ retained**. Action builds slowly over days.
- **Uses:** with loop or thiazide diuretics to prevent potassium loss; oedema of **liver cirrhosis** (high aldosterone) and nephrotic syndrome; **heart failure** (reduces deaths); **primary hyperaldosteronism** (Conn's syndrome); resistant hypertension; hirsutism and acne in women (anti-androgen effect).
- **Adverse effects:** **hyperkalaemia** (dangerous with ACE inhibitors, potassium supplements, kidney failure), **gynaecomastia** and impotence in men, menstrual irregularity.
- Brands: Aldactone; Lasilactone (with frusemide).

### Other potassium-sparing drugs (for comparison)

- **Amiloride** and **triamterene** block the **epithelial sodium channel (ENaC)** in the collecting duct directly; they do not need aldosterone to be present. Used with thiazides or loop diuretics (e.g. amiloride + frusemide) to prevent hypokalaemia. Risk of hyperkalaemia, as with spironolactone.

## 8.7 Osmotic diuretics (for completeness)

- **Mannitol** (a sugar alcohol) is filtered freely but **not reabsorbed**, so it holds water in the tubule by osmosis.
- Given **IV only** (20% solution). Uses: to lower **raised intracranial pressure** and **intraocular pressure** (acute glaucoma), and to maintain urine flow in some kidney emergencies.
- Mannitol 20% solution **crystallises in the cold**; warm the bottle to dissolve crystals and use an in-line filter. Do not use in heart failure or pulmonary oedema (expands blood volume first).

## 8.8 Uses of diuretics at a glance

| Condition | Preferred diuretic | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acute pulmonary oedema | Frusemide IV | Fast and powerful; also dilates veins |
| Chronic heart failure with oedema | Loop diuretic + spironolactone | Removes fluid; spironolactone improves survival |
| Essential hypertension | Thiazide-like (chlorthalidone) | Long action, cheap, proven to reduce strokes |
| Oedema of liver cirrhosis (ascites) | Spironolactone ± frusemide | Aldosterone is high in cirrhosis |
| Oedema with renal failure | Frusemide (high dose) or metolazone | Thiazides fail when GFR is low |
| Glaucoma, mountain sickness | Acetazolamide | Reduces aqueous humour; causes mild acidosis that stimulates breathing |
| Raised intracranial pressure | Mannitol IV | Draws water out of the brain |
| Calcium kidney stones | Thiazide | Reduces urinary calcium |
| Hypercalcaemia | Frusemide + saline | Increases calcium excretion |

## 8.9 Electrolyte effects to remember

| Effect | Loop | Thiazide | Spironolactone | Acetazolamide |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Potassium | ↓ | ↓ | ↑ | ↓ |
| Calcium in urine | ↑ | ↓ | — | — |
| Uric acid in blood | ↑ | ↑ | — | — |
| Blood glucose | ↑ (mild) | ↑ | — | — |
| Acid–base | Alkalosis | Alkalosis | Acidosis (mild) | Acidosis |

## 8.10 Summary table

| Drug | Class / site | Key chemistry | Key use | Key adverse effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Frusemide | Loop, site 2 | Furfuryl anthranilic acid sulphonamide | Acute pulmonary oedema | Hypokalaemia, ototoxicity |
| Bumetanide | Loop | Sulphamoylbenzoic acid | Oedema | As frusemide |
| Benzthiazide | Thiazide, site 3 | Benzothiadiazine | Hypertension, oedema | Hypokalaemia, hyperuricaemia |
| Chlorthalidone | Thiazide-like | Phthalimidine | Hypertension (long acting) | Hypokalaemia |
| Metolazone | Thiazide-like | Quinazolinone | Resistant oedema, low GFR | Hypokalaemia |
| Xipamide | Thiazide-like | Salicylanilide | Oedema | Hypokalaemia |
| Acetazolamide | CA inhibitor, site 1 | Thiadiazole sulphonamide | Glaucoma, mountain sickness | Acidosis, stones |
| Spironolactone | K-sparing, site 4 | Steroid lactone | Cirrhosis, heart failure | Hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia |

**Counselling points for diuretics:** take in the **morning** (avoid night-time urination); eat potassium-rich foods (banana, orange, coconut water) with loop/thiazide diuretics unless also on a potassium-sparing drug; weigh daily in heart failure; stand up slowly.

## Remember

- Loop diuretics block Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ in the thick ascending limb – most powerful (high ceiling).
- Frusemide = 4-chloro-2-furfurylamino-5-sulphamoylbenzoic acid; IV for acute pulmonary oedema; hypokalaemia, ototoxicity; light sensitive.
- Bumetanide ≈ 40 × frusemide potency.
- Thiazides block Na⁺–Cl⁻ in early distal tubule; lose effect at low GFR (except metolazone); chlorthalidone longest acting.
- Acetazolamide = CA inhibitor, mainly glaucoma and mountain sickness.
- Spironolactone = aldosterone antagonist, steroid lactone, K-sparing; hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia.
- Most diuretics are sulphonamides (–SO2NH2).

# Unit 9: Hypoglycaemic agents

**Diabetes mellitus** is a long-term disorder with high blood glucose due to lack of insulin, poor action of insulin, or both.

| | Type 1 | Type 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cause | Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β cells; no insulin | Insulin resistance + gradual β-cell failure |
| Age | Usually young | Usually adults (obesity, family history) |
| Treatment | **Insulin** essential | Diet, exercise, **oral drugs**; insulin later if needed |

**Hypoglycaemic agents** lower blood glucose. The syllabus covers **insulin and its preparations, metformin\*, glibenclamide\*, glimepiride, pioglitazone, repaglinide, gliflozins and gliptins**.

## 9.1 Classification

```text
                    HYPOGLYCAEMIC AGENTS
        ┌──────────────────┴───────────────────────┐
     Insulin                                   Oral / other
  (and analogues)       ┌──────────┬───────────┬──────────┬───────────┬───────────┐
                    Sulphonylureas Biguanides Meglitinides Thiazolidine- DPP-4       SGLT2
                    glibenclamide  metformin  repaglinide  diones       inhibitors  inhibitors
                    glimepiride                            pioglitazone (gliptins)  (gliflozins)
```

| Class | Drugs | Main action | Causes hypoglycaemia alone? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Insulin | Regular, NPH, analogues | Replaces insulin | Yes |
| Sulphonylureas | Glibenclamide, glimepiride, gliclazide, glipizide | ↑ insulin release | **Yes** |
| Biguanides | Metformin | ↓ liver glucose output, ↑ sensitivity | No |
| Meglitinides | Repaglinide, nateglinide | Short burst of insulin release with meals | Yes (less) |
| Thiazolidinediones | Pioglitazone | ↑ insulin sensitivity (PPAR-γ) | No |
| DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins) | Sitagliptin, vildagliptin, saxagliptin, linagliptin, teneligliptin | ↑ incretin (GLP-1) action | No |
| SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins) | Dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, canagliflozin | Glucose lost in urine | No |

## 9.2 Insulin and its preparations

**Insulin** is a polypeptide hormone made by the **β cells of the islets of Langerhans** of the pancreas. It has **51 amino acids** in two chains: **A chain (21)** and **B chain (30)**, joined by **two disulphide bridges** (plus one more disulphide within the A chain).

**Actions:** helps glucose enter muscle and fat cells; promotes glycogen, fat and protein storage; reduces glucose production by the liver.

**Sources:** earlier from beef and pork pancreas; now **human insulin by recombinant DNA technology** (in bacteria or yeast) and **insulin analogues** (amino acid sequence altered to change speed of action).

**Strength:** labelled in **units** (IU). Common strengths: **U-40** (40 units/ml, vials, use U-40 syringes) and **U-100** (100 units/ml, pens and vials). Using the wrong syringe gives a wrong dose.

### 9.2.1 Types of insulin preparations

| Type | Examples | Onset | Duration (approx.) | Appearance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Rapid-acting analogues** | Insulin lispro, aspart, glulisine | 10–20 min | 3–5 h | Clear |
| **Short-acting** | Regular (soluble, plain) insulin | 30–60 min | 6–8 h | Clear |
| **Intermediate-acting** | **NPH (isophane)** insulin – insulin + protamine + zinc; lente (zinc suspension) | 1–2 h | 12–18 h | **Cloudy** (suspension) |
| **Long-acting analogues** | Insulin glargine, detemir, degludec | 1–2 h | ~24 h or more | Clear (glargine) |
| **Premixed** | 30/70 (30% regular + 70% NPH), 50/50 | Biphasic | — | Cloudy |

- Only **clear soluble (regular) insulin** (and some analogues) can be given **intravenously** – used in diabetic ketoacidosis and emergencies.
- Cloudy insulins must be **gently rolled** (not shaken) to mix before use.

### 9.2.2 Uses of insulin

Type 1 diabetes; type 2 not controlled by oral drugs; diabetes in pregnancy; diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar state; diabetic patients during surgery, serious infection; hyperkalaemia (with glucose).

### 9.2.3 Adverse effects

**Hypoglycaemia** (sweating, tremor, palpitations, confusion – treat with oral glucose or IV dextrose/glucagon), weight gain, lipodystrophy at injection sites (rotate sites), allergy (rare with human insulin).

### 9.2.4 Storage of insulin

1. Unopened vials and pens: **refrigerator, 2–8 °C**. **Never freeze** (frozen insulin is spoiled).
2. In-use vial/pen may be kept at room temperature (below about 25–30 °C) for about **4 weeks**, away from heat and sunlight.
3. Do not use if a clear insulin turns cloudy, or if a cloudy insulin has clumps or frosting.
4. During travel use insulated bags; do not keep in a car or checked-in baggage hold.

## 9.3 Biguanides

### Metformin\*

- **Chemical name:** N,N-dimethylbiguanide (3-(diaminomethylidene)-1,1-dimethylguanidine), used as **hydrochloride**.
- **Structure:** a **biguanide** – two guanidine units joined together – with two methyl groups on one terminal nitrogen. Strongly basic, very water-soluble, small molecule.

```text
       H3C              NH        NH
           \            ‖         ‖
            N ──────── C ── NH ── C ── NH2
           /
       H3C
   (two linked guanidine units = biguanide)
```

- **Mechanism:** mainly **reduces glucose production in the liver** (gluconeogenesis), increases glucose uptake by muscles (better insulin sensitivity), reduces glucose absorption from gut. Does **not** increase insulin release, so does **not cause hypoglycaemia** when used alone. Acts partly through activation of AMP-activated protein kinase.
- **Uses:** **first-line drug for type 2 diabetes**, especially overweight patients (no weight gain); polycystic ovarian syndrome; prediabetes.
- **Dose:** usually started at 500 mg once or twice daily with meals, increased gradually (common maximum 2–2.5 g daily in divided doses).
- **Adverse effects:** GI upset (metallic taste, nausea, diarrhoea – reduced by taking with food and starting low); **vitamin B12 deficiency** with long use; rare but serious **lactic acidosis** (risk in kidney failure, liver failure, heart failure, alcoholism, before iodinated contrast dye).
- **Stability/storage:** stable; store in well-closed containers at room temperature.
- **Formulations/brands:** tablets 500 mg, 850 mg, 1 g, sustained-release (SR/ER) tablets; combinations with glimepiride, sitagliptin, vildagliptin, dapagliflozin, pioglitazone. Brands: Glycomet, Glucophage, Obimet.

## 9.4 Sulphonylureas

**Mechanism:** bind the **sulphonylurea receptor** on pancreatic β cells and **close ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels** → depolarisation → Ca²⁺ entry → **insulin release**. Need functioning β cells, so useless in type 1 diabetes.

**General structure:**

```text
   R1 ─ C6H4 ─ SO2 ─ NH ─ C(=O) ─ NH ─ R2
        (benzene)  (sulphonyl) (urea)
```

| Generation | Drugs |
| --- | --- |
| First | Tolbutamide, chlorpropamide (rarely used) |
| Second | **Glibenclamide (glyburide)**, glipizide, gliclazide |
| Third (or later second) | **Glimepiride** |

### Glibenclamide\* (glyburide)

- **Chemical name:** 5-chloro-N-[2-[4-(cyclohexylcarbamoylsulfamoyl)phenyl]ethyl]-2-methoxybenzamide.
- **Structure:** a sulphonylurea: benzene ring bearing –SO2–NH–CO–NH–**cyclohexyl** (R2) on one side and, through an ethyl link, a **5-chloro-2-methoxybenzamide** group (R1) on the other. The large R1 group makes it a potent second-generation drug.
- **Uses:** type 2 diabetes not controlled by diet and metformin.
- **Dose:** usually 2.5–5 mg once daily with breakfast, adjusted; maximum about 15–20 mg/day.
- **Adverse effects:** **hypoglycaemia** (can be prolonged, especially in elderly and in kidney disease – glibenclamide is long acting and has active metabolites), weight gain, GI upset, skin rash.
- **Interactions:** effect increased by alcohol, sulphonamides, some antifungals; β blockers mask warning signs of hypoglycaemia.
- **Storage:** well-closed container, room temperature.
- **Brands:** Daonil, Euglucon (tablets; combinations with metformin).

### Glimepiride

- Sulphonylurea with a pyrroline-carboxamide side chain and a methylcyclohexyl group.
- Once daily; lower risk of hypoglycaemia than glibenclamide; less weight gain.
- Brand: Amaryl, Glimy (alone and with metformin).

## 9.5 Meglitinides

### Repaglinide

- A **benzoic acid** derivative (carbamoylmethyl benzoic acid), non-sulphonylurea.
- Closes K-ATP channels like sulphonylureas, but **acts quickly and briefly**: taken just before each main meal ("one meal, one dose; skip a meal, skip a dose").
- Controls post-meal glucose; less prolonged hypoglycaemia.

## 9.6 Thiazolidinediones (glitazones)

### Pioglitazone

- Contains a **thiazolidine-2,4-dione** ring linked through a benzyl group to an ethylpyridine ether.
- **Mechanism:** activates the nuclear receptor **PPAR-γ** → increases insulin sensitivity in fat, muscle and liver.
- Uses: type 2 diabetes (with metformin or sulphonylurea); slow onset (weeks).
- Adverse effects: **weight gain, fluid retention** (avoid in heart failure), bone fractures, possible bladder cancer risk with long use; liver tests advised.
- Brand: Pioz.

## 9.7 Gliptins (DPP-4 inhibitors)

- After a meal the gut releases **incretins** (GLP-1, GIP), which increase insulin and reduce glucagon in a glucose-dependent way. The enzyme **dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4)** destroys them quickly.
- **Gliptins block DPP-4** → incretin levels rise → better glucose control **without much hypoglycaemia** and **weight neutral**.
- Examples: sitagliptin, vildagliptin, saxagliptin, linagliptin (no dose change in kidney disease), teneligliptin.
- Adverse effects: headache, nasopharyngitis, rare pancreatitis.
- Brands: Januvia (sitagliptin), Galvus (vildagliptin), Trajenta (linagliptin).

## 9.8 Gliflozins (SGLT2 inhibitors)

- **Sodium–glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2)** in the proximal tubule reabsorbs most filtered glucose.
- **Gliflozins inhibit SGLT2** → glucose is passed in the **urine** (glycosuria) → blood glucose falls, with calorie loss (weight loss) and mild diuresis (BP falls).
- Also protect the **heart and kidneys** (reduce heart failure hospitalisation and kidney disease progression).
- Examples: dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, canagliflozin.
- Adverse effects: **genital fungal infections**, urinary tract infections, dehydration, rare ketoacidosis (euglycaemic).
- Brands: Forxiga (dapagliflozin), Jardiance (empagliflozin).

## 9.9 Counselling points

1. Take sulphonylureas with or just before breakfast; never skip meals after taking them.
2. Carry glucose or sugar to treat hypoglycaemia.
3. Metformin with or after food; tell the doctor before contrast X-ray studies.
4. Check blood glucose regularly; HbA1c every 3 months.
5. Foot care, diet and exercise are part of treatment.

## Remember

- Insulin: 51 amino acids, A (21) + B (30) chains, disulphide bonds; regular is clear and can go IV; NPH is cloudy (protamine + zinc); store 2–8 °C, never freeze, in-use ~4 weeks at room temperature.
- Metformin: N,N-dimethylbiguanide; ↓ hepatic glucose; no hypoglycaemia alone; lactic acidosis, B12 deficiency; first line in type 2.
- Glibenclamide: second-generation sulphonylurea (cyclohexyl urea + chloromethoxybenzamide); closes K-ATP channels; prolonged hypoglycaemia.
- Repaglinide: meal-time; pioglitazone: PPAR-γ, fluid retention; gliptins: DPP-4 inhibitors; gliflozins: SGLT2, glucose in urine, genital infections.

# Unit 10: Analgesic and anti-inflammatory agents

An **analgesic** relieves pain without loss of consciousness. Analgesics are of two broad types:

| | Opioid (narcotic) analgesics | Non-opioid analgesics (NSAIDs, paracetamol) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Site | Brain and spinal cord (opioid receptors) | Mainly peripheral (inhibit prostaglandin synthesis) |
| Pain type | Severe pain, visceral pain | Mild to moderate pain, inflammatory pain |
| Anti-inflammatory | No | Yes (except paracetamol) |
| Antipyretic | No | Yes |
| Dependence | Yes | No |

The syllabus covers **morphine analogues, narcotic antagonists and NSAIDs: aspirin\*, diclofenac, ibuprofen\*, piroxicam, celecoxib, mefenamic acid, paracetamol\* and aceclofenac**.

## 10.1 Morphine and its analogues (opioid analgesics)

**Morphine** is the main alkaloid of **opium** (dried latex of the unripe capsules of *Papaver somniferum*). It acts on **μ (mu) opioid receptors** in the brain and spinal cord.

### 10.1.1 Structure of morphine

Morphine is a **pentacyclic** (five-ring) alkaloid containing a **phenanthrene** nucleus partly reduced, an oxygen bridge (furan ring), and a piperidine ring with N-methyl. Important groups:

```text
   Position 3 : phenolic –OH        (methylation → codeine, weaker)
   Position 6 : alcoholic –OH        (oxidation to ketone, or acetylation → more potent)
   Position 7–8 : double bond         (reduction → dihydro compounds)
   Position 17 : N–CH3               (replace by allyl / cyclopropylmethyl → antagonist)
   Ring E : piperidine; 4,5-epoxy (oxygen) bridge
```

**Key features needed for opioid activity (morphine rule):** a tertiary basic nitrogen, a quaternary carbon attached to an aromatic ring, and a two-carbon bridge between them (as in the piperidine ring).

### 10.1.2 Classification of opioids

| Type | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Natural opium alkaloids | Morphine, codeine |
| Semi-synthetic | Diacetylmorphine (heroin), hydromorphone, oxymorphone, oxycodone, buprenorphine |
| Synthetic | Pethidine (meperidine – phenylpiperidine), methadone (diphenylheptane), fentanyl (anilidopiperidine), tramadol |
| Agonist–antagonists | Pentazocine, nalorphine, butorphanol |
| Pure antagonists | Naloxone, naltrexone |

### 10.1.3 Morphine

- **Uses:** severe pain (cancer, myocardial infarction, post-operative, trauma), acute left ventricular failure (pulmonary oedema – relieves breathlessness), pre-anaesthetic.
- **Effects:** analgesia, euphoria, sedation, **respiratory depression**, miosis (pin-point pupils), nausea, constipation, cough suppression, urinary retention, histamine release.
- **Problems:** **tolerance, dependence (addiction)**; overdose → coma, pin-point pupils, respiratory depression (treated with naloxone).
- **Storage and law:** a narcotic drug under the NDPS Act; kept locked; injection protected from light (morphine darkens on oxidation).

### 10.1.4 Morphine analogues

| Drug | Change from morphine / class | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codeine | 3-O-methyl ether of morphine | Cough (antitussive), mild–moderate pain; constipation |
| Diacetylmorphine (heroin) | 3,6-diacetyl ester | Very addictive; not used medically in India |
| Hydromorphone | 6-ketone, 7,8-dihydro | Severe pain (potent) |
| Pethidine | Synthetic phenylpiperidine | Labour pain, post-operative pain; metabolite norpethidine causes fits |
| Methadone | Synthetic, long acting | Opioid de-addiction (substitution), chronic pain |
| Fentanyl | Synthetic, very potent (about 80–100 × morphine) | Anaesthesia, transdermal patch for chronic pain |
| Tramadol | Synthetic, weak μ agonist + inhibits NA/5-HT reuptake | Moderate pain; risk of seizures |

## 10.2 Narcotic (opioid) antagonists

These block opioid receptors and reverse the effects of opioids. Replacing the **N-methyl** of morphine/oxymorphone by an **allyl** or **cyclopropylmethyl** group gives antagonist activity.

| Drug | Chemistry | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Naloxone** | N-allyl-noroxymorphone (14-OH) | Drug of choice for **opioid overdose** (IV/IM/nasal); short acting – may need repeated doses; also reverses opioid respiratory depression in newborns |
| **Naltrexone** | N-cyclopropylmethyl-noroxymorphone | Orally active, long acting; maintenance after opioid detoxification; **alcohol dependence** |
| **Nalorphine** | N-allyl-normorphine | Mixed agonist–antagonist; historical use |

## 10.3 Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

**Mechanism:** NSAIDs inhibit the enzyme **cyclo-oxygenase (COX)**, which converts arachidonic acid into **prostaglandins and thromboxanes**.

```text
   Membrane phospholipids —(phospholipase A2)→ Arachidonic acid
                                                   │ COX-1, COX-2  ← NSAIDs block here
                                                   ↓
                         Prostaglandins (pain, fever, inflammation),
                         thromboxane A2 (platelet aggregation), prostacyclin
```

- **COX-1** (constitutive): protects stomach lining, platelet function, kidney blood flow.
- **COX-2** (inducible): made at sites of inflammation.
- Non-selective NSAIDs block both → effective but cause **gastric irritation/ulcers**; **COX-2 selective** drugs (celecoxib) cause less stomach injury but more cardiovascular risk.

**Actions:** analgesic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory, antiplatelet (aspirin).

**Common adverse effects:** gastric pain, peptic ulcer and bleeding, kidney damage and fluid retention, raised BP, bronchospasm in sensitive asthmatics, rashes. Take after food.

### 10.3.1 Classification (chemical)

| Class | Drugs |
| --- | --- |
| Salicylates | **Aspirin**, sodium salicylate, diflunisal |
| p-Aminophenol derivative | **Paracetamol** (analgesic–antipyretic; very weak anti-inflammatory) |
| Propionic acid derivatives | **Ibuprofen**, naproxen, ketoprofen, flurbiprofen |
| Aryl/heteroaryl acetic acids | **Diclofenac**, **aceclofenac**, indomethacin, ketorolac |
| Anthranilic acids (fenamates) | **Mefenamic acid** |
| Enolic acids (oxicams) | **Piroxicam**, meloxicam |
| Pyrazolones | Metamizole, phenylbutazone |
| COX-2 selective (coxibs) | **Celecoxib**, etoricoxib |

### Aspirin\* (acetylsalicylic acid)

- **Chemical name:** 2-acetoxybenzoic acid (2-(acetyloxy)benzoic acid).
- **Structure:** benzene ring with a **carboxylic acid (–COOH)** and, next to it (ortho), an **acetate ester (–O–CO–CH3)**.

```text
        COOH
        |
     __/__
    /     \── O ── C(=O) ── CH3
    |     |
    \_____/
```

- **Preparation (outline):** salicylic acid + acetic anhydride (with a little H2SO4/H3PO4) → aspirin + acetic acid.
- **Mechanism:** **irreversibly acetylates** a serine in COX; in platelets (which cannot make new enzyme) the effect lasts the platelet's life (7–10 days).
- **Uses and doses:**
  - Pain and fever: 300–600 mg every 4–6 hours (adults).
  - Anti-inflammatory (rheumatic fever): high doses (now rarely).
  - **Antiplatelet:** **75–150 mg once daily** to prevent heart attack and stroke, and after myocardial infarction.
- **Adverse effects:** gastric irritation and bleeding; **Reye's syndrome** in children with viral fever (avoid aspirin in children below 12–16 years except special indications); **salicylism** at high doses (tinnitus, vertigo); aspirin-induced asthma; bleeding tendency.
- **Stability:** in moist air aspirin **hydrolyses** to **salicylic acid and acetic acid** – old tablets smell of **vinegar**. Store in **airtight containers** in a cool dry place. Pharmacopoeia limits **free salicylic acid**.
- **Formulations/brands:** tablets, dispersible tablets (Disprin), enteric-coated low-dose tablets (Ecosprin), combination with clopidogrel or atorvastatin.

### Paracetamol\* (acetaminophen)

- **Chemical name:** N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide (4'-hydroxyacetanilide).
- **Structure:** a **p-aminophenol** derivative: benzene ring with –OH and –NH–CO–CH3 in **para** positions.

```text
   HO ──⟨ benzene ⟩── NH ── C(=O) ── CH3      (para-substituted)
```

- **Mechanism:** inhibits COX mainly in the brain (where peroxide levels are low); weak in inflamed tissues → good analgesic and antipyretic, very weak anti-inflammatory; does not irritate the stomach or affect platelets.
- **Uses and dose:** fever and mild–moderate pain (headache, toothache, body ache, dysmenorrhoea). Adults: **500 mg–1 g every 4–6 hours, not more than 4 g in 24 hours**. Safe in children (dose by weight), pregnancy and peptic ulcer patients.
- **Toxicity:** **overdose causes liver necrosis**. A small part is normally oxidised to the toxic metabolite **NAPQI** (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine), which glutathione detoxifies. In overdose, glutathione is used up and NAPQI damages liver cells. **Antidote: N-acetylcysteine** (best within 8–10 hours). Risk higher in alcoholics and the malnourished.
- **Stability:** stable; store well-closed, protected from light and moisture. Pharmacopoeia limits **4-aminophenol** (hydrolysis product).
- **Formulations/brands:** tablets, syrups, drops, suppositories, IV infusion; Crocin, Calpol, Dolo; with ibuprofen (Combiflam) or other drugs.

### Ibuprofen\*

- **Chemical name:** (RS)-2-(4-isobutylphenyl)propanoic acid (2-[4-(2-methylpropyl)phenyl]propanoic acid).
- **Structure:** a **propionic acid**: benzene ring with an **isobutyl** group at the para position and –CH(CH3)–COOH. The α-carbon is chiral; the **S-(+) isomer is active**, and the R-isomer is partly converted to S in the body; sold as racemate.

```text
   (CH3)2CH–CH2 ──⟨ benzene ⟩── CH(CH3) ── COOH
```

- **Uses and dose:** pain, fever, dysmenorrhoea, rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, soft-tissue injury. Adults commonly 200–400 mg three to four times daily after food.
- **Points:** one of the best tolerated non-selective NSAIDs (less gastric irritation than aspirin at analgesic dose).
- **Storage:** well-closed container.
- **Assay:** acid–base titration with sodium hydroxide in ethanol (it is a carboxylic acid) – done in practicals.
- **Formulations/brands:** tablets, suspension; Brufen, Ibugesic; Combiflam (with paracetamol).

### Diclofenac

- **Chemistry:** 2-[2-(2,6-dichloroanilino)phenyl]acetic acid – a **phenylacetic acid** with a dichlorophenylamino group; used as sodium or potassium salt.
- Potent anti-inflammatory; used in arthritis, back pain, post-operative pain, renal colic; also gel and eye drops.
- Adverse effects: GI, raised liver enzymes, cardiovascular risk. Brand: Voveran.

### Aceclofenac

- **Glycolic acid ester of diclofenac** (–CH2–COO–CH2–COOH); partly converted to diclofenac.
- Claimed better GI tolerance. Used in osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis. Brands: Hifenac, Zerodol.

### Piroxicam

- An **oxicam** (enolic acid, 1,2-benzothiazine with a pyridyl carboxamide).
- **Long half-life (~2 days) → once daily**; more GI side effects.
- Used in rheumatoid and osteoarthritis. Brand: Dolonex.

### Celecoxib

- A **diaryl-substituted pyrazole** carrying a **sulphonamide** group and a trifluoromethyl group.
- **COX-2 selective**: less gastric ulceration but increased risk of heart attack and stroke; avoid in sulpha allergy.
- Used in arthritis, acute pain, dysmenorrhoea. Brand: Celebrex.

### Mefenamic acid

- An **anthranilic acid (fenamate)**: N-(2,3-dimethylphenyl)anthranilic acid.
- Used mainly for **dysmenorrhoea** and menorrhagia, mild pain; diarrhoea is a typical adverse effect. Brand: Meftal.

## 10.4 Summary of starred NSAIDs

| Drug | Class | Chemical name | Key point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Aspirin | Salicylate | 2-acetoxybenzoic acid | Irreversible COX block; 75–150 mg antiplatelet; Reye's syndrome; hydrolyses (vinegar smell) |
| Paracetamol | p-Aminophenol | N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide | No anti-inflammatory action; max 4 g/day; NAPQI liver damage; antidote N-acetylcysteine |
| Ibuprofen | Propionic acid | 2-(4-isobutylphenyl)propanoic acid | S-isomer active; well tolerated |

## Remember

- Morphine: pentacyclic phenanthrene alkaloid; 3-OH phenolic (codeine = 3-methyl ether), 6-OH alcoholic; N-CH3 → N-allyl gives antagonists.
- Naloxone = drug of choice in opioid overdose; naltrexone = oral, long acting (de-addiction, alcoholism).
- NSAIDs block COX → ↓ prostaglandins; COX-1 protects stomach, COX-2 at inflammation; celecoxib COX-2 selective.
- Aspirin: acetylates COX irreversibly; store airtight (hydrolysis → salicylic acid + acetic acid).
- Paracetamol: max 4 g/day; NAPQI; N-acetylcysteine.
- Ibuprofen: propionic acid; diclofenac and aceclofenac: phenylacetic acids; mefenamic acid: fenamate (dysmenorrhoea); piroxicam: oxicam once daily.

# Unit 11: Anti-infective agents

**Anti-infective agents** kill or stop the growth of microbes (fungi, bacteria, mycobacteria, viruses, malaria parasites). This large unit has six groups. Starred drugs: **ketoconazole, fluconazole, ofloxacin, isoniazid (INH), pretomanid, acyclovir, chloroquine phosphate, mefloquine, sulfacetamide and dapsone**.

## 11.1 Antifungal agents

Fungal cell membranes contain **ergosterol** (human cells contain cholesterol). Most antifungals attack ergosterol or its synthesis.

**Classification**

| Class | Drugs | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Polyene antibiotics | Amphotericin B, nystatin | Bind ergosterol → pores in membrane → leakage |
| Heterocyclic benzofuran antibiotic | Griseofulvin | Binds microtubules, stops fungal mitosis |
| Azoles – imidazoles | Miconazole, ketoconazole, clotrimazole | Inhibit **lanosterol 14α-demethylase** (a CYP450 enzyme) → no ergosterol |
| Azoles – triazoles | Fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole | Same, more selective for fungal enzyme |
| Allylamines | Naftifine, terbinafine | Inhibit **squalene epoxidase** |

### Amphotericin B

- **Polyene macrolide** antibiotic from *Streptomyces nodosus*.
- Drug of choice for serious **systemic fungal infections** (cryptococcal meningitis, invasive candidiasis, aspergillosis) and **mucormycosis**; also kala-azar.
- Given by slow **IV infusion** (not absorbed orally). **Nephrotoxicity**, fever and chills during infusion, low potassium. **Liposomal** forms are less toxic.
- **Storage:** powder in the **refrigerator (2–8 °C), protected from light**; reconstitute with water/dextrose (precipitates in saline).

### Griseofulvin

- From *Penicillium griseofulvum*; oral, for **dermatophyte** infections of skin, hair and nails (tinea); deposits in new keratin. Take with a **fatty meal** (better absorption). Long course (weeks–months). Not effective on Candida.

### Miconazole

- Imidazole; mainly **topical** (cream, powder, oral gel, vaginal) for candidiasis and tinea.

### Ketoconazole\*

- **Chemical name:** cis-1-acetyl-4-[4-[[2-(2,4-dichlorophenyl)-2-(1H-imidazol-1-ylmethyl)-1,3-dioxolan-4-yl]methoxy]phenyl]piperazine.
- **Structure:** an **imidazole** ring and a **2,4-dichlorophenyl** group on a **1,3-dioxolane** ring, which is linked by –CH2–O– to a phenyl ring carrying an **N-acetylpiperazine**.
- **Uses:** now mainly **topical**: dandruff and seborrhoeic dermatitis (2% shampoo), tinea and pityriasis versicolor (cream). Oral use is restricted because of **liver toxicity**; it also inhibits human steroid synthesis (gynaecomastia) and many CYP enzymes (drug interactions) – oral form occasionally used in Cushing's syndrome.
- **Points:** needs acid for oral absorption.
- **Brands:** Nizral (cream, shampoo), Ketostar.

### Fluconazole\*

- **Chemical name:** 2-(2,4-difluorophenyl)-1,3-bis(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)propan-2-ol.
- **Structure:** a propan-2-ol whose central carbon carries –OH and a **2,4-difluorophenyl** ring; each end carbon carries a **1,2,4-triazole** ring.

```text
                  OH
                  |
   triazole–CH2 ─ C ─ CH2–triazole
                  |
             2,4-difluorophenyl
```

- **Points:** water soluble, well absorbed orally (also IV), long half-life (once daily), enters **CSF** well, excreted unchanged in urine; fewer interactions and less liver toxicity than ketoconazole.
- **Uses:** vaginal candidiasis (**single 150 mg oral dose**), oral and oesophageal thrush, cryptococcal meningitis, systemic candidiasis, prophylaxis in immunocompromised patients.
- **Brands:** Forcan, Zocon, Flucos (tablets, IV infusion, eye drops).

### Itraconazole

- Triazole; oral (with food) for **dermatophytes, onychomycosis**, aspergillosis, histoplasmosis. Brand: Canditral.

### Naftifine hydrochloride

- **Allylamine**; inhibits squalene epoxidase; topical cream for tinea.

## 11.2 Urinary tract anti-infective agents (fluoroquinolones)

**Quinolones** are synthetic antibacterials. Adding **fluorine at position 6** and a **piperazine at position 7** of the 4-quinolone ring gave the **fluoroquinolones**, which are broad spectrum.

**Mechanism:** inhibit bacterial **DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II)** and **topoisomerase IV** → bacteria cannot coil and separate DNA → bactericidal.

**Basic structure (4-quinolone-3-carboxylic acid)**

```text
   4-Quinolone nucleus: benzene ring (A) fused to a pyridone ring (B)

     N-1  : ethyl or cyclopropyl (ofloxacin: bridged to C-8 by –O–CH2–CH(CH3)–)
     C-3  : –COOH  ┐  together bind DNA gyrase
     C-4  : =O     ┘  (and chelate Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Al³⁺, Fe²⁺ → antacid interaction)
     C-6  : –F        (fluorine → "fluoro"quinolone, broad spectrum)
     C-7  : piperazine ring (anti-pseudomonal activity, better tissue spread)
```

| Drug | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Norfloxacin | Low blood levels; used for **urinary tract** and GI infections |
| Ciprofloxacin | N1-cyclopropyl; UTI, typhoid, gonorrhoea, respiratory, bone infections; most active against Gram-negatives |
| **Ofloxacin\*** | Tricyclic; good oral absorption; UTI, respiratory, typhoid, eye/ear drops, leprosy and TB regimens |
| Moxifloxacin | Better against Gram-positive and anaerobes ("respiratory quinolone"); MDR-TB |

### Ofloxacin\*

- **Chemical name:** (±)-9-fluoro-2,3-dihydro-3-methyl-10-(4-methylpiperazin-1-yl)-7-oxo-7H-pyrido[1,2,3-de]-1,4-benzoxazine-6-carboxylic acid.
- **Structure:** a **tricyclic** fluoroquinolone: the quinolone ring is bridged from N-1 to C-8 by an –O–CH2–CH(CH3)– chain (forming a benzoxazine ring); it has the **carboxylic acid, ketone, fluorine** and **N-methylpiperazine** groups. It is a **racemate**; the active **S-(−) isomer is levofloxacin**.
- **Uses:** urinary tract infections, respiratory and soft-tissue infections, typhoid, gonorrhoea (earlier), eye and ear infections, leprosy and tuberculosis regimens.
- **Adverse effects (fluoroquinolones):** nausea, dizziness, **tendon rupture**, QT prolongation, photosensitivity; **avoid in children and pregnancy** (cartilage damage in young animals).
- **Interaction:** absorption is reduced by **antacids, iron, calcium, zinc** (chelation) – give 2 hours apart.
- **Storage:** protect from light.
- **Brands:** Zanocin, Oflox (tablets, infusion, eye/ear drops).

## 11.3 Anti-tubercular agents

**Tuberculosis** (TB) is caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It needs **combination therapy for months** to cure and to prevent resistance. **First-line drugs: isoniazid (H), rifampicin (R), pyrazinamide (Z), ethambutol (E)**; streptomycin (S) was also first line. Under India's National TB Elimination Programme, new cases receive **2 months HRZE + 4 months HRE** (daily, fixed-dose combinations).

**MDR-TB** (resistant to at least H and R) and **XDR-TB** need second-line and newer drugs (bedaquiline, delamanid, pretomanid, linezolid, fluoroquinolones).

| Drug | Chemistry | Mechanism | Key adverse effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Isoniazid (INH)\*** | Pyridine-4-carbohydrazide | Inhibits **mycolic acid** synthesis (cell wall) | Peripheral neuropathy, hepatitis |
| Rifampicin | Semisynthetic rifamycin (macrocyclic) | Inhibits bacterial **DNA-dependent RNA polymerase** | Hepatitis, **orange-red urine/tears**, enzyme induction (reduces contraceptive effect) |
| Pyrazinamide | Pyrazine-2-carboxamide | Active in acid medium inside macrophages | Hepatotoxicity, **raised uric acid (gout)** |
| Ethambutol | Ethylenediamine dibutanol (D-isomer) | Inhibits arabinogalactan synthesis (cell wall) | **Optic neuritis** (red–green colour vision loss) – avoid in young children who cannot report vision |
| Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) | 4-amino-2-hydroxybenzoic acid | Folate synthesis inhibitor (PABA analogue) | GI upset; second line |
| Bedaquiline | **Diarylquinoline** | Inhibits mycobacterial **ATP synthase** | QT prolongation; MDR-TB |
| Delamanid | Nitro-dihydro-imidazo-oxazole | Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis | QT prolongation; MDR-TB |
| **Pretomanid\*** | Nitroimidazo-oxazine | Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis; releases nitric oxide in non-growing bacilli | Liver injury, peripheral neuropathy, myelosuppression (with linezolid) |

### Isoniazid\* (INH)

- **Chemical name:** pyridine-4-carbohydrazide (isonicotinic acid hydrazide).
- **Structure:** a **pyridine** ring with a **–CO–NH–NH2** (carbohydrazide) group at position 4.

```text
          N
       //   \
      |      |
       \\   /
          C4 ── C(=O) ── NH ── NH2
```

- **Mechanism:** a **prodrug** activated by the mycobacterial enzyme **KatG**; inhibits synthesis of **mycolic acids** of the cell wall. Bactericidal for multiplying bacilli.
- **Uses:** all forms of TB (part of every first-line regimen); **TB preventive therapy** (contacts, HIV-positive persons).
- **Adverse effects:** **peripheral neuropathy** (INH causes **pyridoxine** deficiency – give **vitamin B6 10–25 mg/day** to prevent it), **hepatitis** (more with age, alcohol and rifampicin), rash, fits in overdose. **Slow acetylators** keep higher levels (more neuropathy).
- **Interactions:** inhibits metabolism of phenytoin (toxicity).
- **Storage:** protect from light.
- **Brands:** Isokin; part of FDC tablets (e.g. Akurit, Rifa-I-6).

### Pretomanid\*

- **Chemical name:** (6S)-2-nitro-6-{[4-(trifluoromethoxy)benzyl]oxy}-6,7-dihydro-5H-imidazo[2,1-b][1,3]oxazine.
- **Structure:** a **nitroimidazole** ring fused to a **dihydro-oxazine** ring (bicyclic nitroimidazo-oxazine), with a **4-(trifluoromethoxy)benzyloxy** side chain; one chiral centre (S).
- **Mechanism:** a prodrug activated by a mycobacterial nitroreductase; inhibits mycolic acid synthesis in growing bacilli and releases **reactive nitrogen species (nitric oxide)** that kill dormant bacilli.
- **Uses:** with **bedaquiline and linezolid** (the "**BPaL**" regimen; BPaLM adds moxifloxacin) for **drug-resistant (MDR/XDR) pulmonary TB**, over about 6 months.
- **Adverse effects:** liver injury, peripheral and optic neuropathy, anaemia and low blood counts (mostly from linezolid), QT prolongation with bedaquiline.

## 11.4 Antiviral agents

Viruses live inside host cells, so few drugs are selective. Most antivirals are **nucleoside analogues** that block viral nucleic acid synthesis.

| Drug | Chemistry | Mechanism | Uses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Amantadine hydrochloride | **Adamantane** (cage-like tricyclic) amine | Blocks influenza A **M2 ion channel** (uncoating); also releases dopamine | Influenza A (rarely now – resistance); **Parkinsonism** |
| Idoxuridine | 5-Iodo-2'-deoxyuridine (thymidine analogue) | Gets into viral DNA | **Topical** for herpes simplex keratitis (too toxic systemically) |
| **Acyclovir\*** | Acyclic guanosine analogue | Viral DNA polymerase inhibitor / chain terminator | Herpes simplex, varicella-zoster |
| Foscarnet | Pyrophosphate analogue (trisodium phosphonoformate) | Directly blocks viral DNA polymerase | CMV retinitis, acyclovir-resistant herpes; nephrotoxic |
| Zidovudine (AZT) | 3'-azido-3'-deoxythymidine | **Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor** (NRTI) | **HIV** (with other antiretrovirals), prevention of mother-to-child transmission; bone marrow suppression (anaemia) |
| Ribavirin | Synthetic guanosine-like nucleoside (triazole carboxamide) | Interferes with viral RNA synthesis | RSV (aerosol), hepatitis C (with others), Lassa fever; haemolytic anaemia, teratogenic |
| Remdesivir | Adenosine nucleotide analogue **prodrug** | Inhibits viral **RNA-dependent RNA polymerase** | COVID-19 (IV, hospitalised patients) |
| Favipiravir | Pyrazinecarboxamide derivative (prodrug) | Inhibits viral RNA polymerase | Influenza; was used for mild COVID-19 in some countries |

### Acyclovir\* (aciclovir)

- **Chemical name:** 2-amino-9-[(2-hydroxyethoxy)methyl]-1,9-dihydro-6H-purin-6-one.
- **Structure:** **guanine** (a purine base) attached at N-9 to an **acyclic** side chain –CH2–O–CH2–CH2–OH that mimics an incomplete deoxyribose sugar (no 3'-OH).

```text
        guanine ring (purine)
              |
              N9 ── CH2 ── O ── CH2 ── CH2 ── OH
                    (acyclic "sugar": no ring, no 3'-OH)
```

- **Mechanism:** phosphorylated first by **viral thymidine kinase** (so it is activated only in infected cells – selective), then by host enzymes to acyclovir triphosphate, which inhibits viral DNA polymerase and is incorporated into viral DNA, causing **chain termination** (no 3'-OH to add the next nucleotide).
- **Uses:** genital and oral herpes, herpes keratitis (ointment), **herpes zoster (shingles)**, chickenpox in high-risk patients, herpes encephalitis (IV), prophylaxis in transplant patients.
- **Adverse effects:** usually mild (headache, nausea); IV can cause **crystalluria/renal damage** (keep patient hydrated, infuse slowly).
- **Points:** poor oral absorption (prodrug **valacyclovir** gives higher levels).
- **Brands:** Zovirax, Acivir (tablets, cream, eye ointment, IV).

## 11.5 Antimalarials

Malaria is caused by *Plasmodium* (in India mainly *P. falciparum* and *P. vivax*), spread by female *Anopheles* mosquitoes.

**Classification by chemistry**

| Class | Drugs |
| --- | --- |
| Cinchona alkaloid (quinoline methanol) | **Quinine** |
| 4-Aminoquinoline | **Chloroquine**, amodiaquine |
| 8-Aminoquinoline | **Primaquine**, tafenoquine |
| Quinoline methanol (synthetic) | **Mefloquine** |
| Biguanide / dihydrotriazine | Proguanil → active metabolite **cycloguanil** |
| Diaminopyrimidine | **Pyrimethamine** (with sulfadoxine) |
| Sesquiterpene lactone endoperoxide | **Artemisinin** and derivatives (artesunate, artemether, arteether) |

**By stage of action:** blood schizonticides (chloroquine, quinine, mefloquine, artemisinins) cure the attack; **tissue schizonticides** (primaquine) kill liver forms (hypnozoites) to prevent **relapse** in vivax; **gametocides** (primaquine) stop spread.

### Chloroquine phosphate\*

- **Chemical name:** N4-(7-chloroquinolin-4-yl)-N1,N1-diethylpentane-1,4-diamine (as diphosphate).
- **Structure:** a **quinoline** ring with **Cl at position 7** and, at position 4, an amino group carrying a branched diethylaminopentyl side chain (4-aminoquinoline).

```text
   quinoline ring
     C-7 : Cl
     C-4 : NH ─ CH(CH3) ─ CH2CH2CH2 ─ N(C2H5)2
```

- **Mechanism:** concentrates in the parasite's food vacuole and stops conversion of toxic haem into harmless **haemozoin** → parasite dies.
- **Uses:** **vivax** malaria (with primaquine for radical cure); falciparum only where sensitive (widespread resistance); **extra-intestinal amoebiasis**; rheumatoid arthritis and lupus (hydroxychloroquine preferred).
- **Adverse effects:** bitter taste, nausea, **itching** (common in Africans/Indians), headache; long-term high doses → **retinopathy**; IV bolus dangerous (hypotension).
- **Storage:** well-closed, protected from light; keep away from children (overdose is very toxic).
- **Brands:** Lariago, Resochin (tablets, syrup, injection).

### Primaquine phosphate

- 8-Aminoquinoline. Kills liver hypnozoites → **radical cure of vivax** (14 days); single low dose to kill falciparum gametocytes.
- **Causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency** – test where possible; not in pregnancy or infants.

### Quinine sulphate

- Main alkaloid of **cinchona bark**; quinoline-methanol with a quinuclidine ring.
- Severe/complicated falciparum (IV, when artesunate unavailable), resistant malaria (oral with doxycycline/clindamycin), nocturnal leg cramps.
- **Cinchonism** (tinnitus, deafness, vertigo, nausea), hypoglycaemia (stimulates insulin release).

### Mefloquine\*

- **Chemical name:** [2,8-bis(trifluoromethyl)quinolin-4-yl](piperidin-2-yl)methanol (as hydrochloride; racemic).
- **Structure:** a **quinoline methanol** related to quinine: quinoline ring with **two CF3 groups (positions 2 and 8)**; at position 4 a –CH(OH)– linking to a **2-piperidyl** ring.
- **Uses:** treatment of uncomplicated chloroquine-resistant falciparum malaria (with artesunate); **prophylaxis** for travellers (weekly dosing because of long half-life).
- **Adverse effects:** **neuropsychiatric** (vivid dreams, anxiety, depression, psychosis, seizures), dizziness, cardiac conduction changes; avoid in epilepsy and psychiatric illness.
- **Brand:** Mefliam (tablets).

### Cycloguanil, pyrimethamine, artemisinin

- **Cycloguanil** (dihydrotriazine) – active form of proguanil; inhibits plasmodial **dihydrofolate reductase**.
- **Pyrimethamine** – diaminopyrimidine DHFR inhibitor; combined with sulfadoxine (sequential block of folate synthesis) as **SP**, used with artesunate in India; with sulfadiazine for toxoplasmosis.
- **Artemisinin** – from *Artemisia annua* (qinghaosu); **endoperoxide bridge** generates free radicals inside the parasite. Fastest-acting antimalarial. Used as **artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT)**: artesunate + SP, artemether + lumefantrine. IV artesunate is the drug of choice for severe malaria.

## 11.6 Sulphonamides and sulphones

**Sulphonamides** are synthetic **analogues of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA)**. Bacteria must make their own folic acid from PABA; sulphonamides **competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase** → no folic acid → bacteriostatic. Humans take ready-made folic acid from food, so are not affected.

**Basic structure (sulphanilamide)**

```text
   H2N ──⟨ benzene ⟩── SO2 ── NH ── R
   (N4: free amino           (N1: R varies – heterocycles
    group, must be para       increase potency and
    to the SO2 group)         change solubility)
```

**SAR:** the free **para-amino group (N4)** is essential (or a group that becomes amino in the body); the sulphur must be directly on the benzene ring; substituting N1 with heterocyclic rings (pyrimidine, isoxazole) gives more active drugs.

| Drug | N1 substituent / chemistry | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sulphanilamide | –H (parent compound) | Historical |
| Sulphadiazine | Pyrimidin-2-yl | Toxoplasmosis (with pyrimethamine); silver sulphadiazine cream for burns |
| Sulphamethoxazole | 5-Methylisoxazol-3-yl | With trimethoprim |
| **Sulphacetamide\*** | Acetyl | **Eye infections** (eye drops) |
| Mafenide acetate | Homosulphanilamide (–CH2NH2 instead of –NH2; not a PABA antagonist) | Burns cream (works in pus) |
| Cotrimoxazole | Sulphamethoxazole + trimethoprim (5 : 1) | UTI, respiratory infections, **Pneumocystis pneumonia**, typhoid |
| **Dapsone\*** | Sulphone (not a sulphonamide) | **Leprosy** |

**Adverse effects of sulphonamides:** **crystalluria** (drink plenty of water; alkaline urine), allergic rashes including **Stevens–Johnson syndrome**, haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, kernicterus in newborns (displace bilirubin – avoid near term and in neonates).

**Cotrimoxazole:** sulphamethoxazole blocks dihydropteroate synthase; **trimethoprim** blocks **dihydrofolate reductase** – **sequential blockade**, bactericidal combination. Brands: Septran, Bactrim.

### Sulphacetamide\* (sulfacetamide sodium)

- **Chemical name:** N-[(4-aminophenyl)sulfonyl]acetamide (used as sodium salt).
- **Structure:** sulphanilamide with an **acetyl group on N1** (–SO2–NH–CO–CH3).
- **Points:** the sodium salt is very **water soluble** and gives a nearly neutral solution that does not irritate the eye much; penetrates eye tissues.
- **Uses:** **conjunctivitis, corneal ulcer, trachoma, ophthalmia neonatorum** (10–30% eye drops, eye ointment).
- **Stability/storage:** eye drops darken on long storage/light exposure (discard discoloured solution); store **protected from light**, tightly closed; use within the stated period after opening.
- **Brands:** Albucid, Locula (eye drops).

### Dapsone\*

- **Chemical name:** 4,4'-sulfonyldianiline (bis(4-aminophenyl) sulphone; diaminodiphenyl sulphone, DDS).
- **Structure:** two **p-aminophenyl** rings joined by a **sulphone (–SO2–)** group.

```text
   H2N ──⟨ benzene ⟩── SO2 ──⟨ benzene ⟩── NH2
```

- **Mechanism:** like sulphonamides, inhibits folate synthesis (PABA antagonist).
- **Uses:** **leprosy** (with rifampicin and clofazimine in multidrug therapy), **dermatitis herpetiformis**, prevention of *Pneumocystis* pneumonia in HIV (alternative to cotrimoxazole).
- **Adverse effects:** **haemolytic anaemia** (especially G6PD deficiency), methaemoglobinaemia, "dapsone syndrome" (fever, rash, hepatitis), lepra reactions.
- **Storage:** protect from light.
- **Brands:** Dapsone tablets; part of leprosy MDT blister packs.

## Remember

- Polyenes bind ergosterol (amphotericin B, IV, nephrotoxic, refrigerate); azoles block 14α-demethylase; allylamines block squalene epoxidase.
- Ketoconazole: imidazole + dioxolane + acetylpiperazine; oral restricted (liver); topical shampoo. Fluconazole: bis-triazole difluorophenyl propanol; CSF, 150 mg single dose for vaginal candidiasis.
- Fluoroquinolones: 6-F, 7-piperazine, 3-COOH, 4-oxo; DNA gyrase; ofloxacin tricyclic racemate (levofloxacin = S); no antacids; avoid in children.
- INH = pyridine-4-carbohydrazide; neuropathy → pyridoxine; HRZE. Pretomanid: nitroimidazo-oxazine, BPaL for drug-resistant TB.
- Acyclovir: acyclic guanine; activated by viral thymidine kinase; chain terminator.
- Chloroquine: 7-Cl 4-aminoquinoline (vivax, amoebiasis, retinopathy); primaquine: 8-aminoquinoline (radical cure, G6PD haemolysis); mefloquine: 2,8-bis-CF3 quinoline methanol (neuropsychiatric); artemisinin: endoperoxide, ACT.
- Sulphonamides: PABA analogues, need free para-NH2; crystalluria. Sulphacetamide = N1-acetyl, eye drops. Dapsone = diaminodiphenyl sulphone, leprosy, G6PD haemolysis.

# Unit 12: Antibiotics

An **antibiotic** is, strictly, a substance produced by a micro-organism that kills or inhibits other micro-organisms in low concentration (e.g. penicillin from *Penicillium*, streptomycin from *Streptomyces*). Today the word also covers their semi-synthetic and synthetic relatives. The syllabus lists **penicillin G, amoxicillin\*, cloxacillin, streptomycin, tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline), macrolides (erythromycin, azithromycin) and miscellaneous (chloramphenicol\*, clindamycin)**.

## 12.1 Classification of antibiotics

**By mechanism of action**

| Target | Antibiotics |
| --- | --- |
| Cell wall synthesis | β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems), vancomycin |
| Protein synthesis – 30S ribosome | Aminoglycosides (streptomycin), tetracyclines |
| Protein synthesis – 50S ribosome | Macrolides (erythromycin, azithromycin), chloramphenicol, clindamycin, linezolid |
| Nucleic acid synthesis | Rifampicin, fluoroquinolones |
| Cell membrane | Polymyxins, polyenes |
| Folate synthesis | Sulphonamides, trimethoprim |

**By chemical class**

| Class | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| β-Lactams | Penicillin G, amoxicillin, cloxacillin, cephalexin |
| Aminoglycosides | Streptomycin, gentamicin, amikacin |
| Tetracyclines | Tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline |
| Macrolides | Erythromycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin |
| Amphenicols | Chloramphenicol |
| Lincosamides | Clindamycin, lincomycin |

**Bactericidal** (kill): β-lactams, aminoglycosides. **Bacteriostatic** (stop growth): tetracyclines, macrolides, chloramphenicol, clindamycin.

## 12.2 Penicillins (β-lactam antibiotics)

### 12.2.1 Structure of penicillins

All penicillins share **6-aminopenicillanic acid (6-APA)**: a **β-lactam ring** (four-membered cyclic amide) fused to a **thiazolidine ring** (five-membered, containing S and N). Different acyl side chains (R–CO–) on the 6-amino group give different penicillins.

```text
            R ─ C(=O) ─ NH ─ C6 ─── C5 ─── S
                             |       |      \
                             C7 ─── N4       C(CH3)2
                             ‖        \      /
                             O         C3 ─
                                       |
                                       COOH
   C7=O + N4 + C5 + C6 = β-lactam ring (4-membered)
   N4, C5, S, C(CH3)2, C3 = thiazolidine ring (5-membered)
```

**Mechanism:** the strained β-lactam ring acylates (binds) the **penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases)** that cross-link peptidoglycan in the bacterial cell wall. The wall becomes weak and the bacterium bursts (bactericidal, works on growing bacteria). Human cells have no cell wall, so penicillins are very safe.

**Weak points:**

1. **Acid** – destroys some penicillins in the stomach (penicillin G).
2. **β-Lactamase (penicillinase)** – bacterial enzyme that opens the β-lactam ring → resistance.
3. **Allergy** – the commonest problem (rash to anaphylaxis); always ask about penicillin allergy; cross-allergy among all penicillins.

**Classification of penicillins**

| Group | Drugs | Feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Natural | Penicillin G (benzylpenicillin), penicillin V | Narrow spectrum; G acid-labile |
| Penicillinase-resistant | **Cloxacillin**, flucloxacillin, methicillin | Bulky side chain protects β-lactam ring |
| Aminopenicillins (extended spectrum) | Ampicillin, **amoxicillin** | Also cover some Gram-negatives |
| Antipseudomonal | Piperacillin, carbenicillin | Pseudomonas |
| With β-lactamase inhibitors | Amoxicillin + **clavulanic acid**; piperacillin + tazobactam | Inhibitor protects the penicillin |

### Penicillin G (benzylpenicillin)

- Side chain: **phenylacetyl** (benzyl). Natural, from *Penicillium chrysogenum*.
- **Acid-labile** (given IM/IV), destroyed by penicillinase, short half-life (prolonged by probenecid; depot forms procaine and **benzathine penicillin**).
- Uses: streptococcal infections (pharyngitis, cellulitis), pneumococcal infections, **syphilis**, meningococcal meningitis, diphtheria, tetanus, gas gangrene, **prevention of rheumatic fever** (benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks).
- Stability: dry powder is stable; **solution after reconstitution is unstable** – use soon (store as directed). Unit dose expressed in **units** (lakh units).

### Amoxicillin\*

- **Chemical name:** (2S,5R,6R)-6-[[(2R)-2-amino-2-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetyl]amino]-3,3-dimethyl-7-oxo-4-thia-1-azabicyclo[3.2.0]heptane-2-carboxylic acid (used as trihydrate).
- **Structure:** 6-APA nucleus with a **D-(−)-α-amino-p-hydroxyphenylacetyl** side chain. It is ampicillin with an extra **–OH at the para position** of the phenyl ring.

```text
   HO ──⟨ benzene ⟩── CH(NH2) ── C(=O) ── NH ── [6-APA nucleus]
         (p-hydroxy)  (α-amino group → Gram-negative activity
                        and acid stability)
```

- **Points:** **acid stable** (oral); **better absorbed than ampicillin** and not affected much by food; broad spectrum (streptococci, pneumococci, *H. influenzae*, *E. coli*, *Salmonella*, *H. pylori*); destroyed by β-lactamase (so combined with **clavulanic acid**).
- **Uses:** respiratory tract infections, otitis media, sinusitis, UTI, typhoid (sensitive strains), **H. pylori** eradication (with clarithromycin + a proton pump inhibitor), dental infections, endocarditis prophylaxis.
- **Adverse effects:** diarrhoea, allergy; **rash in infectious mononucleosis**.
- **Stability/storage:** capsules/tablets in a cool dry place; **dry syrup** for children is reconstituted with water just before use and then kept in a refrigerator and used within about **7 days** (as labelled); shake well.
- **Brands:** Mox, Novamox (capsules, dry syrup); Augmentin, Moxikind-CV (with clavulanic acid).

### Cloxacillin

- **Isoxazolyl penicillin**: side chain carries a 3-(2-chlorophenyl)-5-methylisoxazole group. The bulky group **shields the β-lactam ring from penicillinase**.
- **Acid stable** (oral) and penicillinase-resistant, but narrow spectrum.
- Uses: **penicillinase-producing *Staphylococcus aureus*** infections (boils, abscesses, osteomyelitis); combined with ampicillin/amoxicillin. Not active against MRSA.
- Brand: Klox.

## 12.3 Aminoglycosides – Streptomycin

- From *Streptomyces griseus* (Waksman, 1944) – first drug effective against **TB**.
- **Chemistry:** aminoglycoside – amino sugars (streptose, N-methyl-L-glucosamine) linked by glycosidic bonds to an aminocyclitol (**streptidine**). Highly polar, basic, water soluble.
- **Mechanism:** binds the **30S ribosomal subunit** → misreading of mRNA → faulty proteins; bactericidal.
- **Not absorbed orally** → given **IM** (TB) or IV for other aminoglycosides.
- **Uses:** tuberculosis (now mainly in drug-resistant regimens), plague, tularaemia, with penicillin in enterococcal endocarditis (historically).
- **Adverse effects:** **ototoxicity** – mainly **vestibular** (giddiness, imbalance) with streptomycin; **nephrotoxicity**; neuromuscular blockade; avoid in pregnancy (fetal deafness).
- **Storage:** dry powder vials at room temperature; reconstituted solution under refrigeration for a short time.

## 12.4 Tetracyclines

- **Chemistry:** a **four-ring (tetracyclic) naphthacene** (octahydronaphthacene) nucleus with many –OH, keto and a dimethylamino group, and a carboxamide.
- **Mechanism:** bind the **30S subunit** and block attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA → bacteriostatic.
- **Broad spectrum:** Gram-positive, Gram-negative, rickettsiae, chlamydia, mycoplasma, cholera, some protozoa (malaria prophylaxis/treatment), acne bacteria.

| Drug | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Doxycycline** | Long acting (once/twice daily), well absorbed, can be used in kidney failure; uses: respiratory infections, cholera, rickettsial fevers (**scrub typhus**), leptospirosis, acne, chlamydia, malaria (prophylaxis, with quinine), Lyme disease. Brand: Doxy-1 |
| **Minocycline** | Most lipid soluble; acne, meningococcal carriers; vestibular side effects (dizziness), skin pigmentation |

**Adverse effects of tetracyclines**

1. **Teeth discolouration** (yellow-brown) and bone deposition – **avoid in children below 8 years and in pregnancy/breastfeeding**.
2. GI irritation, **oesophageal ulcers** (swallow with full glass of water, stay upright).
3. **Photosensitivity**.
4. Superinfection (candidiasis, diarrhoea).
5. Liver damage in pregnancy (high IV doses).

**Interaction:** tetracyclines **chelate calcium, magnesium, aluminium, iron, zinc** → do not take with **milk, antacids or iron tablets** (doxycycline less affected than older tetracyclines).

**Stability:** **outdated/degraded tetracycline** (epi-anhydrotetracycline formed by heat, moisture and acid) can damage the kidneys (**Fanconi syndrome**). Store in tight, light-resistant containers, cool and dry; never use expired tetracyclines.

## 12.5 Macrolides

- **Chemistry:** a large **macrocyclic lactone ring** (14-membered in erythromycin and clarithromycin; **15-membered "azalide"** in azithromycin, with a nitrogen in the ring) attached to deoxy sugars (desosamine, cladinose).
- **Mechanism:** bind the **50S subunit** and block translocation → bacteriostatic.
- **Spectrum:** Gram-positive cocci, *Mycoplasma*, *Chlamydia*, *Legionella*, *Bordetella* (whooping cough), *Campylobacter*.

| | Erythromycin | Azithromycin |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source | *Saccharopolyspora* (formerly *Streptomyces*) *erythraea* | Semi-synthetic from erythromycin |
| Ring | 14-membered | 15-membered (azalide) |
| Acid stability | **Acid-labile** – given as enteric-coated tablets or stable esters/salts (estolate, stearate, ethylsuccinate) | Acid stable |
| Half-life / dosing | Short; 4 times a day | **Very long tissue half-life**; once daily, **3–5 day course** |
| GI upset | Common (motilin agonist) | Less |
| Interactions | Inhibits CYP3A4 (raises levels of other drugs) | Few |
| Uses | Penicillin-allergy alternative, whooping cough, diphtheria carriers | Respiratory infections, typhoid, chlamydial infections (single dose), trachoma, community-acquired pneumonia |
| Brands | Erythrocin, Althrocin | Azithral, Azee |

Erythromycin **estolate** can cause cholestatic jaundice. Macrolides can prolong the QT interval.

## 12.6 Miscellaneous antibiotics

### Chloramphenicol\*

- **Chemical name:** 2,2-dichloro-N-[(1R,2R)-1,3-dihydroxy-1-(4-nitrophenyl)propan-2-yl]acetamide.
- **Structure:** a **p-nitrophenyl** ring attached to a propane-1,3-diol chain; the C-2 nitrogen carries a **dichloroacetyl** group. Two chiral centres; only the **D-(−)-threo (1R,2R)** isomer is active. Unusual for a natural product to contain a nitro group and chlorine.

```text
   O2N ──⟨ benzene ⟩── CH(OH) ── CH ── CH2OH
                                  |
                                  NH ── C(=O) ── CHCl2
```

- **Source:** first isolated from *Streptomyces venezuelae*; now made **synthetically** (the first antibiotic to be fully synthesised commercially).
- **Mechanism:** binds the **50S** subunit, inhibits peptidyl transferase → bacteriostatic; broad spectrum including anaerobes, rickettsiae, *Salmonella typhi*, *H. influenzae*.
- **Uses:** now limited because of toxicity – **bacterial conjunctivitis and eye infections** (eye drops/ointment), ear drops, serious infections when alternatives fail (meningitis in penicillin allergy, typhoid in resistant cases, brain abscess).
- **Adverse effects:** **bone marrow depression** – dose-related reversible anaemia and rare **fatal aplastic anaemia** (unpredictable, even after eye drops); **grey baby syndrome** in newborns (the immature liver cannot conjugate it → cyanosis, collapse); enzyme inhibition (raises phenytoin, warfarin levels).
- **Stability/formulation:** intensely **bitter** – the tasteless **palmitate ester** is used for oral suspensions; the water-soluble **sodium succinate ester** for injection. Both are hydrolysed in the body to active chloramphenicol. Eye drops are stored in a **refrigerator (2–8 °C)** before opening because the solution slowly loses potency; protect from light.
- **Brands:** Chloromycetin; Chlorocol eye drops.

### Clindamycin

- **Lincosamide** (7-chloro-7-deoxy derivative of lincomycin).
- Binds the **50S** subunit; active against Gram-positive cocci (including some MRSA) and **anaerobes** (*Bacteroides*).
- Uses: anaerobic infections (abdominal, pelvic, lung abscess), bone and joint infections, dental infections, **acne** (topical gel), toxoplasmosis, malaria (with quinine).
- Adverse effect: **antibiotic-associated (pseudomembranous) colitis** due to *Clostridioides difficile* – stop drug if severe diarrhoea.
- Brand: Dalacin C.

## 12.7 Rational antibiotic use (counselling)

1. Take the full course even after feeling better.
2. Do not use antibiotics for viral colds and flu.
3. Keep correct timing (spacing doses); some with food, some on empty stomach.
4. Avoid milk/antacids/iron with tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.
5. Report rash, breathing difficulty, severe diarrhoea at once.
6. Misuse leads to **antimicrobial resistance** (AMR) – a major public health problem; antibiotics are Schedule H/H1 drugs, sold only on prescription.

## Remember

- Penicillin nucleus = 6-APA: β-lactam + thiazolidine; acts on transpeptidases (cell wall); problems: acid, penicillinase, allergy.
- Penicillin G: acid-labile, IM/IV; benzathine for rheumatic fever prophylaxis.
- Amoxicillin: p-hydroxy ampicillin; acid stable, well absorbed; + clavulanic acid; dry syrup 7 days in fridge after mixing.
- Cloxacillin: isoxazolyl, penicillinase-resistant (staph).
- Streptomycin: aminoglycoside, 30S, IM; vestibular ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity; TB.
- Tetracyclines: 4-ring naphthacene, 30S; teeth staining (avoid < 8 years, pregnancy); chelation; expired → Fanconi syndrome. Doxycycline once daily.
- Macrolides: 50S; erythromycin acid-labile, 14-ring; azithromycin 15-ring azalide, once daily 3–5 days.
- Chloramphenicol: p-nitrophenyl + dichloroacetamide, D-threo; aplastic anaemia, grey baby; palmitate (taste) and succinate (injection) esters; eye drops in fridge.
- Clindamycin: lincosamide, anaerobes, pseudomembranous colitis.
